label: Roaring Twenties
pitch:
In 1918 the guns of the World War go silent and a soldier-borne flu kills more Americans than the war did. Eleven years later, on a single October afternoon, the New York stock market falls off a cliff and takes the decade with it. In between is the Roaring Twenties: the first modern consumer economy, the first broadcast nation, the first car culture — and, running on the exact same calendar, the largest peacetime nativist movement in American history.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The 1918–19 influenza pandemic killed roughly 675,000 Americans in under a year — more than every U.S. combat death in the World War, World War II, Korea, and Vietnam combined
• At its 1924–25 peak the second Ku Klux Klan claimed four to five million members and effectively controlled the politics of Indiana, Oregon, and Colorado — it was a national, not a Southern, movement
• On May 21, 1927, Charles Lindbergh landed outside Paris after 33.5 hours alone in a single-engine plane, and an estimated four million people turned out for his New York ticker-tape parade — the largest crowd in the city's history to that point
• Between Black Thursday and Black Tuesday (October 24–29, 1929), the stock market lost about $30 billion in two weeks, roughly ten times the federal budget and more than the entire cost of the World War to the United States

🤔 Why It Matters: The twenties built the America that came after it. Mass production, installment credit, national advertising, the radio network, the Hollywood studio, the suburb, and the modern celebrity were all assembled in this decade and have never been disassembled. So was the modern culture war: the Scopes 'Monkey' Trial, Prohibition, immigration restriction by national origin, and the Klan were a coordinated backlash against everything the boom represented, and that argument never really ended. The decade also proved, expensively, that a stock market detached from the economy underneath it is a bubble, and that nobody in charge will say so until it bursts.

🎲 Wild Card: The decade's defining business was illegal. Prohibition didn't end drinking; it handed a multibillion-dollar industry to organized crime, which used the profits to build the modern American Mafia. Al Capone's Chicago operation grossed an estimated $60 million a year, paid no taxes, ran the city's police and aldermen, and was finally brought down not for the St. Valentine's Day Massacre but for failing to file a tax return — the one law a bootlegger could not buy his way around.

details.label: Background
details.text: The United States entered the World War in April 1917 and shipped two million men to France by the armistice of November 1918. The country that won the war was a great industrial power with no plan for what to do with itself afterward.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: An influenza pandemic killed roughly 675,000 Americans. Wartime price controls came off into a brutal inflation, four million workers struck in 1919, and the Bolshevik Revolution abroad triggered the First Red Scare, the Palmer Raids, and mass deportations. White mobs attacked Black communities in the Red Summer of 1919 and destroyed the Greenwood district of Tulsa in 1921.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The boom that gave the decade its name was preceded by two years of plague, strikes, race massacres, and political terror, and a sharp depression in 1920–21. The 'return to normalcy' Warren Harding campaigned on in 1920 was a promise to make the previous three years stop.

details.label: Background
details.text: Warren Harding, an amiable Ohio newspaper publisher and senator, won the 1920 election in the largest popular-vote landslide to that point on a platform of doing less. He filled the cabinet with a mix of genuine talents and Ohio cronies.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Andrew Mellon began cutting the top income-tax rate, the economy recovered fast, and immigration restriction began with the 1921 Emergency Quota Act. Meanwhile the 'Ohio Gang' looted the government: the Teapot Dome oil-lease bribery became the worst federal corruption scandal before Watergate. Harding died suddenly in August 1923 before most of it surfaced.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Harding's death turned a mediocre, scandal-ridden presidency into a martyrdom and handed a clean, silent Vermonter the White House at the exact moment the boom took off.

details.label: Background
details.text: Calvin Coolidge took the oath by lamplight on his father's Vermont farm, said as little as possible, and let business run. 'The chief business of the American people is business.'

details.label: What Happened
details.text: The Mellon tax cuts, mass production, installment credit, electrification, and national advertising produced the first modern consumer economy. Cars, radios, movies, and appliances reached the mass market. The 1924 Johnson–Reed Act slammed the immigration door, the second Klan peaked and then collapsed, and the Scopes trial staged the culture war on the radio.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Real, broad, and unequal: farmers, Black Americans, and the coal and textile regions never got the boom, and the prosperity was increasingly running on debt. Coolidge 'did not choose to run' in 1928 and left office before the bill came due.

details.label: Background
details.text: A generation came home from the war, the Nineteenth Amendment enfranchised women, the Great Migration moved more than a million Black Americans north, and radio and records carried the new music everywhere at once.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Jazz went national through Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and Bessie Smith. The Harlem Renaissance produced Hughes, Hurston, McKay, and Locke's 'The New Negro,' Marcus Garvey's mass movement, and the NAACP's anti-lynching campaign. F. Scott Fitzgerald named the age and Hemingway and the Lost Generation rewrote American prose.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The decade's permanent cultural legacy was made by the people the decade's politics were trying to suppress — Black musicians, immigrant filmmakers, and a generation of writers in open revolt against the official optimism.

details.label: Background
details.text: After the 1926 collapse of the Florida land boom, speculative money moved to Wall Street. Herbert Hoover, the celebrated engineer-administrator, won the 1928 election in another landslide promising the 'final triumph over poverty.'

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Stock prices roughly doubled in two years on a flood of borrowed 'margin' money and leveraged investment trusts. The market peaked on September 3, 1929, wobbled, and then crashed on Black Thursday, Black Monday, and Black Tuesday in late October.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The Crash did not by itself cause the Great Depression, but it ended the decade's defining illusion: that the boom was permanent and the prosperity general. What the Depression and the next war reshaped is the subject of the narratives that follow.

events.label: Armistice ends the World War
events.description: At 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918, Germany signed an armistice in a railroad car in Compiègne Forest, ending four years of fighting on the Western Front. Americans celebrated in the streets — many of them unknowingly inside the second wave of the deadliest flu pandemic in modern history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The armistice terms were so punishing that Germany had no real choice: it was collapsing from within, with naval mutinies and the Kaiser about to abdicate. The signing car itself became a symbol of national humiliation for Germans, a grievance that Hitler would exploit — and he staged France's 1940 surrender in the same car, in the same clearing.

events.label: 1918 influenza pandemic
events.description: The 1918 influenza pandemic killed roughly 675,000 Americans and 50–100 million worldwide — more than the war itself. Uniquely, it targeted healthy young adults: a vigorous immune response could flood the lungs until the patient essentially drowned in their own fluid.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'Spanish flu' name stuck not because it originated in Spain but because neutral Spain's uncensored press reported it while the warring nations suppressed the news. The earliest documented U.S. cases appeared in March 1918 in Haskell County, Kansas. Philadelphia's disastrous Liberty Loan parade on September 28, 1918 — held over public-health objections — became the textbook case of what not to do: within weeks the city's hospitals were overwhelmed and the dead outran the supply of coffins.

events.label: Wilson's Fourteen Points & Versailles
events.description: President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points were his blueprint for a postwar peace, outlined in January 1918, with a League of Nations at the center. The Senate refused to ratify the Versailles Treaty that included the League, leaving the United States outside the international body it had proposed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wilson's closest Allied partners — Britain's Lloyd George and France's Clemenceau — were privately skeptical of his idealism from the start, and haggled away much of the Fourteen Points at the Paris negotiations. Wilson suffered a severe stroke in October 1919 while barnstorming the country to build public support for the treaty, leaving him an invalid for the rest of his term.

events.label: Eighteenth Amendment ratified
events.description: The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified January 16, 1919, wrote a nationwide ban on the manufacture, sale, and transport of alcohol into the U.S. Constitution — the first amendment in history to restrict a personal freedom rather than secure one, and the only amendment ever repealed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Congress proposed the amendment in December 1917 and it needed three-quarters of states to ratify; 46 of the then-48 states ultimately did, making it appear nearly unanimous. Repeal came just shy of 14 years later via the Twenty-first Amendment in December 1933, making it the shortest-lived constitutional amendment. No other amendment has ever been repealed.

events.label: Seattle General Strike
events.description: For five days in February 1919, all 65,000 organized workers in Seattle walked out together — the first general strike (a city-wide work stoppage, not just one trade) in U.S. history — in solidarity with locked-out shipyard workers demanding higher wages.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The strike was strikingly disciplined: strikers organized their own milk deliveries and kept public order themselves, and the whole thing ended peacefully in less than a week. Despite the calm, Seattle's mayor Ole Hanson declared it an attempted revolution and rode the 'I stopped the Bolsheviks' story to national fame — proof that political optics often matter more than what actually happened.

events.label: The 1919 strike wave
events.description: 1919 was the largest strike year in American history: roughly four million workers — about one in five in the entire workforce — walked off the job at some point, driven by wartime wage freezes that had left real pay far behind rising prices.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Almost every major 1919 strike ended in defeat. The Great Steel Strike, with 350,000 workers, was broken with private guards, court injunctions, and a press campaign that painted its organizers as Bolshevik agents. Union membership, which had risen during the war, then fell steadily through the entire prosperous decade that followed — meaning the twenties boom was built, in part, on organized labor's rout.

events.label: Boston Police Strike
events.description: On September 9, 1919, Boston's police walked off the job seeking union recognition and better pay, leaving the city with several nights of looting. Massachusetts Governor Calvin Coolidge broke the strike, refused to rehire the officers, and issued a single line — 'There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time' — that put him on the 1920 Republican ticket.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Police Commissioner Edwin Upton Curtis had provoked the strike by refusing to allow officers to affiliate with the AFL, arguing that a unionized police force could not be trusted to protect city officials and business interests. The strikers were never rehired; Boston recruited an entirely new force. Coolidge's national fame from the incident was so immediate that he went from obscure state governor to Vice President within a year.

events.label: Red Summer of 1919
events.description: In the summer and fall of 1919, white mobs attacked Black communities in more than three dozen cities across the United States in what civil rights leader James Weldon Johnson named the 'Red Summer' — red for blood.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Johnson, an NAACP field secretary, organized peaceful protests in response as the violence unfolded. A crucial difference from earlier waves of racist violence: many of the Black men in these cities were recently returned World War I veterans who were armed and fought back, a shift that unsettled white communities that had counted on one-sided violence. The Red Summer intensified the Great Migration northward rather than stopping it, because for many the rural South looked worse.

events.label: Chicago race riot of 1919
events.description: After a Black teenager named Eugene Williams was stoned and drowned for drifting across an unwritten color line at a Lake Michigan beach on July 27, 1919, eight days of violence left 38 dead and between 1,000 and 2,000 Black residents — most of them Black — burned out of their homes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Two-thirds of the 537 recorded injuries were to Black Chicagoans; one-third to white. The riot lasted from July 27 to August 3 and was considered the worst of the Red Summer disturbances nationwide. A subsequent investigation found that Chicago's segregated housing conditions and the competition for factory jobs between Black migrants and white workers (many of them recent European immigrants) were the structural fuel; the beach incident was the match.

events.label: Anarchist bombing campaign
events.description: From April through June 1919, followers of Italian anarchist Luigi Galleani mailed and detonated bombs aimed at prominent politicians and businessmen — a real, coordinated campaign of political violence that helped ignite the Red Scare.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Almost all of the bombs were sent by mail; postal workers actually intercepted most of them before delivery. The June night bombings hit eight cities simultaneously, and the bomber who struck Attorney General Palmer's house on R Street in Washington blew himself up on the front steps. Despite the coordinated scale, only two people were killed total — but the psychological impact was enormous and handed Palmer a political rationale for the mass raids that followed.

events.label: First Red Scare
events.description: After Russia's 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, Americans feared the upheaval would jump the Atlantic. In 1919–20, radicals, immigrants, and labor organizers were bundled together as a single revolutionary threat, triggering the First Red Scare — a panic that did far more damage than the actual threat warranted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The First Red Scare grew from a collision of real events: the Russian Revolution, the German Revolution of 1918–19, and a genuine wave of anarchist bombings on U.S. soil. At its height the fear was less about communism as a doctrine and more about the sheer visible number of immigrants arriving from exactly the places the revolution was coming from. The crackdown it licensed reached well beyond any actual threat, suppressing labor activism, deporting immigrants, and hardening nativist sentiment that would soon close the immigration door entirely.

events.label: The Palmer Raids
events.description: In November 1919 and January 1920, Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer and his 24-year-old aide J. Edgar Hoover orchestrated mass arrests of suspected radicals across 36 cities — around 6,000 people seized, mostly without warrants, mostly immigrants, with hundreds ultimately deported.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The raids targeted Italian and Eastern European Jewish immigrants with particular intensity. Though Palmer arrested thousands, his deportation drive was repeatedly frustrated by the Labor Department, which controlled deportation authority and objected to his methods — only 556 foreign citizens were ultimately deported. Hoover, running the Justice Department's new 'radical division,' built the filing and surveillance machinery during the raids that he would use to monitor Americans for the next half-century as FBI director.

events.label: The 'Soviet Ark' deportations
events.description: In December 1919, the army transport Buford — gleefully dubbed the 'Soviet Ark' by the press — sailed for Soviet Russia carrying 249 deported radicals, the most famous of them being anarchist writer Emma Goldman.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Goldman had lived in the United States since 1885 and had spent decades agitating for labor rights, free speech, and birth control, making her arguably the most famous radical in the country. She was deported not after a criminal conviction but through an administrative immigration hearing — no jury, no requirement to prove a crime — the legal shortcut Palmer had refined into a mass-deportation tool. The Buford itself had originally been built in 1890 as the SS Mississippi and was a veteran Army transport from the Spanish–American War.

events.label: ACLU founded
events.description: The American Civil Liberties Union was founded in 1920 specifically to do what no organization had reliably done before: put lawyers in front of anyone whose speech or political associations the government was punishing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ACLU grew directly out of an earlier wartime organization, the National Civil Liberties Bureau, which had defended conscientious objectors during World War I. Felix Frankfurter was among the prominent lawyers who helped give it intellectual credibility from the start. Within five years of founding it was defending a Tennessee teacher named Scopes for teaching evolution — a case that became the decade's most public test of whether the state could police what went on in a classroom.

events.label: Sacco and Vanzetti arrested
events.description: In May 1920, Italian immigrant anarchists Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were arrested for a payroll robbery and double murder in South Braintree, Massachusetts, setting off a seven-year legal battle that became the Red Scare era's most contested case.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The robbery took place on April 15, 1920, at the Slater and Morrill Shoe Company; both men were armed when arrested and lied to police about their movements. The victims were a guard and a paymaster. Most historians now consider the 1921 trial unfair — the defendants' anarchism and immigrant backgrounds were used against them throughout — though modern ballistics re-analysis has left the question of Sacco's guilt genuinely unresolved.

events.label: Wall Street bombing
events.description: At noon on September 16, 1920, a horse-drawn wagon packed with dynamite and 500 pounds of iron weights detonated directly in front of the J.P. Morgan bank on Wall Street, killing 38 people instantly and wounding hundreds more — the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil to that point.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The bomb killed 30 people instantly; eight more died of their wounds, with 143 seriously injured and hundreds more hurt. The attack was never solved — investigators suspected the Galleanist anarchists but made no arrests. Workers cleaned up the scene and the Stock Exchange reopened the next morning; Morgan's chose to leave the shrapnel scars in the building's limestone facade, where they remain today.

events.label: Nineteenth Amendment ratified
events.description: Ratified on August 18, 1920, after a seventy-year campaign, the Nineteenth Amendment barred states from denying the vote on account of sex, making roughly 26 million American women eligible to vote in the November 1920 presidential election.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tennessee was the decisive 36th state, and the margin was razor-thin: the state house vote was tied until 24-year-old legislator Harry Burn switched from no to yes after his mother wrote him urging him to 'be a good boy' and vote for ratification — a letter Burn himself cited as the reason for his switch. The amendment removed sex as a barrier but left intact the poll taxes, literacy tests, and outright violence Southern states used to block Black voters, meaning most Black women in the South still could not vote in 1920.

events.label: League of Women Voters founded
events.description: Carrie Chapman Catt founded the League of Women Voters in 1920, weeks before the Nineteenth Amendment was certified, to help newly enfranchised women become informed voters. It represented the moderate wing of suffrage's aftermath, focused on civic participation rather than further constitutional change.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The LWV was a direct successor to the National American Woman Suffrage Association, which Catt had led. The organization immediately split from Alice Paul's militant wing, which wanted to push straight on to an Equal Rights Amendment; Catt and the LWV worried the ERA would void the protective labor laws that working-class women depended on. That same rift between equality-feminism and protective-legislation-feminism would run through the women's movement for the rest of the century.

events.label: Volstead Act takes effect
events.description: The Volstead Act (formally the National Prohibition Act, 1919) was the enforcement law for the Eighteenth Amendment, defining 'intoxicating liquor' as anything over half a percent alcohol — a threshold so low it banned even weak beer. Drafted by Anti-Saloon League strategist Wayne Wheeler, it was named after Minnesota congressman Andrew Volstead.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The act was named not for its author but for Judiciary Committee chairman Andrew Volstead, who shepherded it through the House — the actual drafter, Wayne Wheeler, stayed deliberately behind the scenes. Funding was kept so thin that the entire federal Prohibition enforcement force never exceeded a few thousand agents to police a country of 120 million people, making the law structurally unenforceable from day one.

events.label: Warren Harding elected
events.description: Ohio senator Warren G. Harding won the 1920 presidential election with about 60 percent of the popular vote — the largest landslide to that point — on a promise of 'normalcy' after years of war, flu, and Progressive-era crusading. It was the first nationwide election in which women could vote.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Harding's running mate was Massachusetts governor Calvin Coolidge, who had come to national attention crushing the Boston police strike the previous year. The Democratic ticket paired Ohio governor James M. Cox with a young assistant Navy secretary named Franklin D. Roosevelt — a future president losing badly to a future bad president.

events.label: KDKA goes on the air
events.description: On November 2, 1920, a Westinghouse engineer in a Pittsburgh rooftop shack read election returns into a microphone over KDKA, the first commercially licensed radio broadcast in the United States. A few hundred people with homemade crystal sets heard it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: KDKA's call letters were assigned by the navy's licensing system, which had regulated ship radio before commercial broadcasting existed. Westinghouse had built the station partly to sell radio receivers; broadcasting the election was essentially a marketing stunt. The station is still on the air today, making it one of the longest continuously operating commercial radio stations in the world.

events.label: Depression of 1920–21
events.description: When war contracts evaporated overnight after the armistice, the U.S. economy lurched through a brief inflationary surge in 1919–20 and then a sharp deflationary crash: prices collapsed, farm income cratered, and unemployment climbed toward 12 percent by 1921.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The slump ran from roughly January 1920 to July 1921 — about 18 months — and the federal government's response was almost nothing by modern standards: the Federal Reserve raised interest rates, the Treasury ran a surplus, and the bust simply burned itself out. The hands-off recovery became a favorite example for small-government economists arguing that downturns self-correct if left alone.

events.label: Emergency Quota Act of 1921
events.description: The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 was the first numerical cap on European immigration, limiting each nationality to 3 percent of its U.S.-resident population as counted in the 1910 census — a formula deliberately designed to favor long-established northern and western Europeans over the newer southern and eastern wave.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before 1921 there were no numerical limits on European immigration at all; the new law represented a structural break in U.S. policy, not just a tightening. The 3-percent/1910-census formula was considered a stopgap — restrictionists immediately complained it was still too generous because so many southern and eastern Europeans had already arrived by 1910. It was marked explicitly as temporary legislation, yet its two innovations (numerical caps and the quota-per-nationality structure) proved permanent and became the template for every subsequent immigration law through 1965.

events.label: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.description: On May 31–June 1, 1921, a white mob — deputized and armed by the city of Tulsa itself — destroyed the Greenwood district, a prosperous Black neighborhood known as 'Black Wall Street,' killing an estimated 100–300 people and leaving 10,000 homeless.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The massacre destroyed more than 35 square blocks, including hotels, law offices, a hospital, and a library — institutions that had made Greenwood one of the wealthiest Black communities in the United States. The city of Tulsa actively suppressed the event for fifty years: no prosecutions, no insurance payouts, the records buried, the massacre kept out of local textbooks. A 2001 Oklahoma state commission concluded the city bore direct responsibility; ongoing archaeological excavations searching for mass graves continue to turn up remains.

events.label: The Great Migration
events.description: Between roughly 1916 and 1930, more than 1.5 million Black Americans fled Jim Crow, debt, and lynching in the rural South for the factory cities of the North and Midwest — the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Black press, especially the Chicago Defender, was so effective at advertising Northern opportunity that white planters in many Southern towns banned and confiscated it; Pullman porters smuggled bundles south and dropped them along the rail line to be passed hand to hand. Isabel Wilkerson, who wrote the definitive history, describes it as a collective 'declaration of independence' — migrants were not fleeing randomly but choosing, deliberately, to leave.

events.label: Rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan
events.description: The second Klan was refounded at a ceremony on Stone Mountain, Georgia, in 1915 — the same year 'The Birth of a Nation' rehabilitated the first Klan on screen — and after 1920 professional promoters turned it into a slick, dues-charging, multi-million-member national fraternal order targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as much as Black Americans.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Promoters Edward Young Clarke and Elizabeth Tyler ran the Klan's expansion like a sales business, keeping a cut of every initiation fee (called a 'klectoken') and every robe sale. The Klan's hooded costume itself was not a Reconstruction tradition but was lifted directly from the 1915 film. By 1924 it had chapters in every state, including chapters in cities like Chicago, Denver, and Portland that dwarfed most Southern klaverns.

events.label: Shuffle Along opens on Broadway
events.description: Written and performed by Black artists, the musical Shuffle Along ran for 504 Broadway performances in 1921 and launched a vogue for Black theater. It helped open white audiences and producers to the Harlem Renaissance about to flower uptown.

events.label: Marcus Garvey and the UNIA
events.description: Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association built the largest Black mass movement in American history around racial pride, economic self-sufficiency, and the dream of return to Africa — its 1920 New York convention drew tens of thousands of delegates from across the diaspora.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Garvey was Jamaican-born but built his American base from Harlem, launching a newspaper (the Negro World), a shipping line (the Black Star Line), and plans for an African nation. He declared himself Provisional President of Africa — a title that reads as grandiose but carried enormous symbolic weight for followers who had never been offered political dignity by any government.

events.label: First Mellon tax cut
events.description: Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon — Pittsburgh banker, aluminum and oil magnate, one of the three or four richest Americans — launched his decade-long tax-cutting program with the Revenue Act of 1921, arguing that high wartime rates drove wealthy investors into tax-exempt shelters instead of productive investment.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mellon served as Treasury Secretary under three consecutive presidents — Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover — an unusually long tenure that let him carry the same policy through an entire economic cycle. His personal art collection, assembled while he was cutting taxes on the rich, eventually became the founding collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

events.label: Washington Naval Conference
events.description: The Washington Naval Conference (November 1921 – February 1922), hosted by Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, produced the first arms-control treaty in history, capping the battleship tonnage of the U.S., Britain, Japan, France, and Italy at fixed ratios and effectively ending a naval arms race.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hughes opened the conference by announcing that the United States would scrap 30 ships — including 15 already under construction — a proposal so dramatic that a British admiral said it sank more ships in 35 minutes than all the admirals in the world had in a century. The resulting 5:5:3 tonnage ratio (U.S., Britain, Japan) was Japan's price for accepting a smaller fleet: the other powers agreed not to build new naval bases in the Pacific.

events.label: Reader's Digest founded
events.description: DeWitt and Lila Wallace launched Reader's Digest in 1922, condensing articles for busy readers. With Time (1923) and the tabloids, it was part of a new mass-circulation media built for a hurried, national audience.

events.label: Sinclair Lewis publishes Babbitt
events.description: Sinclair Lewis's 1922 novel Babbitt skewered the conformist, booster, business-obsessed American middle class so precisely that 'babbitt' became a common noun — a type, not just a character — and helped earn Lewis the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1930.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The novel's protagonist George Babbitt is a real-estate agent in the fictional Midwestern city of Zenith, which Lewis based on cities like Cincinnati and Minneapolis after careful sociological research. Lewis was the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, and the Nobel committee specifically cited Babbitt and its social satire as central to the award. The novel was filmed twice in the silent era and remade as a talkie in 1934.

events.label: Fordney–McCumber Tariff
events.description: The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff raised import duties to protect American manufacturers and farmers. It signaled the decade's economic nationalism and helped choke the international trade that war-debtor Europe needed to repay the United States.

events.label: Teapot Dome scandal
events.description: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased the Navy's oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, and Elk Hills, California — set aside to fuel the fleet in wartime — to private oilmen without competitive bidding, in exchange for roughly $400,000 in cash, loans, and cattle.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Senate investigation that exposed the scandal was triggered partly because Fall suddenly paid off his debts and renovated his New Mexico ranch after years of financial distress — a senator noticed. The oil reserves had been transferred from the Navy Department to the Interior Department just months before Fall leased them, a transfer Fall had quietly arranged.

events.label: The Ohio Gang
events.description: Harding's circle of Ohio poker buddies and political cronies — nicknamed the 'Ohio Gang' by the press — treated the federal government as a revenue source, selling pardons, Prohibition exemptions, government contracts, and access to confiscated liquor out of a K Street house in Washington.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The gang's headquarters was an unmarked house at 1625 K Street NW where Attorney General Harry Daugherty's friend Jess Smith ran the operation — cashing in on pardons and immunity deals. Smith, apparently fearing exposure, died of a gunshot in 1923, ruled a suicide; Daugherty was tried twice for conspiracy but never convicted.

events.label: Veterans' Bureau scandal
events.description: Charles Forbes, Harding's director of the brand-new Veterans' Bureau — the agency meant to care for men disabled in the World War — looted it through kickbacks on hospital construction contracts and the fraudulent sale of medical supplies, with estimated losses around $200 million.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Forbes sold government-owned medical supplies — bandages, drugs, bedsheets — to a Boston contractor at pennies on the dollar and collected kickbacks; warehouses full of goods meant for veterans were stripped. Harding reportedly grabbed Forbes by the throat when he learned of the theft, but let him flee to Europe before forcing his resignation.

events.label: Equal Rights Amendment introduced
events.description: Alice Paul (who had chained herself to the White House fence to win the vote) drafted the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 with Crystal Eastman and had it introduced in Congress, aiming to constitutionally ban sex discrimination in all its forms.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ERA split the women's movement immediately: labor feminists, backed by unions and the League of Women Voters, argued it would strike down hard-won laws limiting women's working hours and banning them from dangerous night work. The amendment was reintroduced every Congress for nearly 50 years before finally passing both chambers in 1972 — and then stalled three states short of ratification, where it still sits.

events.label: Time magazine launched
events.description: Henry Luce and Briton Hadden launched Time in March 1923 as a weekly news digest for the busy modern reader. It pioneered a brisk, opinionated national news style and built one of the great twentieth-century media empires.

events.label: Death of President Harding
events.description: Warren Harding died suddenly in San Francisco on August 2, 1923, most likely of a heart attack, while on a speaking tour of the West. He died beloved; the full scale of his administration's corruption surfaced only in the years after.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Harding died before the Teapot Dome scandal became public, which meant the country mourned him as a well-meaning president cut down too soon — a reputation that collapsed within two years. His death was so sudden and unexpected that Vice President Calvin Coolidge learned he was president from a messenger who drove to his father's farm in Vermont in the middle of the night, and his father — a notary public — administered the oath of office by lamplight.

events.label: Coolidge sworn in by lamplight
events.description: Calvin Coolidge was vacationing at his father's Vermont farmhouse when a midnight messenger brought word that Harding had died. His father, John, being a notary public (a local official legally empowered to administer oaths), swore him in by kerosene lamp at 2:47 a.m. — the only time in American history a president was sworn in by his own father.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: John Coolidge's authority to administer the oath was briefly questioned afterward, and Coolidge quietly took a second oath from a federal judge just to be safe. The Plymouth Notch farmhouse had no telephone, meaning news of Harding's death traveled by car up a dark dirt road. Coolidge was the 30th president and the second vice president after Theodore Roosevelt to ascend mid-term and then win a full term in his own right.

events.label: The Dawes Plan
events.description: American banker Charles Dawes engineered a 1924 plan to reschedule German war reparations and pump U.S. loans into Germany, which paid reparations to Britain and France, which repaid war debts to the U.S. The circular flow held until 1929.

events.label: Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson–Reed)
events.description: The Johnson–Reed Act of 1924 made immigration restriction permanent, cutting the quota to 2 percent and rewinding the baseline to the 1890 census — a year before the mass southern and eastern European wave — so the arithmetic itself would lock out Italians, Poles, Greeks, and Jews while giving Britain and Germany the lion's share of slots.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 1924 act also created the U.S. Border Patrol and established the 'consular control system,' requiring immigrants to obtain a visa from a U.S. consulate abroad before traveling — shifting the screening gate overseas so unwanted migrants never boarded ships in the first place. The law's designers were explicit: congressional committee reports cited eugenic 'expert testimony' about the hereditary inferiority of southern and eastern European 'stocks' to justify the 1890 baseline. Italy, which had been sending hundreds of thousands of immigrants a year, was cut to roughly 4,000 annually.

events.label: Indian Citizenship Act
events.description: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted U.S. citizenship to all Native Americans born in the country — a status the Fourteenth Amendment had theoretically promised but treaty-sovereignty exceptions had long denied. It passed the same Congress that was racially sorting out the rest of the world's immigrants.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The act was partly motivated by the service of some 12,000 Native Americans who had fought in World War I, including many who had enlisted before they were even citizens. But citizenship did not automatically carry voting rights: several states, including Arizona and New Mexico, continued to bar Native Americans from voting through state constitutional provisions until 1948, and some local barriers persisted well into the 1950s and 1960s. Tribes had not been consulted about the legislation, and some leaders opposed it, arguing that imposed U.S. citizenship threatened tribal sovereignty and treaty relationships.

events.label: Coolidge elected in his own right
events.description: Calvin Coolidge won the 1924 presidential election on the slogan 'Keep Cool with Coolidge,' running against a Democratic Party that had shattered itself at its convention and a Progressive third-party challenger, Senator Robert La Follette, who pulled nearly five million votes but carried only his home state of Wisconsin.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: La Follette's five million votes were the best third-party showing since Theodore Roosevelt's 1912 run — a sign of how much discontent existed even in a boom year. The Democrats' 1924 convention in New York took 103 ballots to pick a candidate, exhausting delegates and the public alike. Coolidge's running mate, Charles G. Dawes, had just won the Nobel Peace Prize for his plan to restructure Germany's WWI reparations payments.

events.label: Klan march on Washington
events.description: On August 8, 1925, between 30,000 and 50,000 white-robed Klansmen marched in daylight down Pennsylvania Avenue past the Capitol — the high-water mark of the second Klan, a national mass movement that claimed four to five million members at its peak.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The marchers deliberately removed or covered their hoods for much of the route to prove they had nothing to hide, turning the march into a declaration of mainstream respectability rather than secrecy. The second Klan had more members in Indiana alone than in any Southern state. The 1925 march drew participants from as far as Oregon and Colorado, underscoring that the organization's strongholds were in the North and Midwest, not the old Confederacy.

events.label: The Stephenson scandal and Klan collapse
events.description: D.C. Stephenson, the Klan's Grand Dragon for Indiana who had handpicked the state's governor and much of its legislature, was convicted of second-degree murder in November 1925 after abducting and savagely assaulting a young woman named Madge Oberholtzer, who died from her injuries; when the politicians he had bought refused to pardon him, he handed prosecutors his corruption records and brought the whole machine down with him.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Oberholtzer's deathbed statement, given before she died, was admitted as evidence and described the assault in graphic detail — it was read aloud in a courtroom packed with reporters and became a national scandal. Stephenson served 25 years before his 1950 parole. Indiana Klan membership, roughly 250,000 at its peak, had effectively collapsed to a few thousand within two years of the conviction.

events.label: The Scopes 'Monkey' Trial
events.description: In July 1925, biology teacher John Scopes was put on trial in Dayton, Tennessee for teaching human evolution in violation of state law — a case the town deliberately staged for the publicity and that the ACLU paid for as a constitutional test. The eight-day spectacle, carried live on national radio, pitted the country's most famous lawyer against its most famous orator and turned into the decade's great public argument about science versus faith.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Scopes himself wasn't sure he had ever actually taught evolution — he incriminated himself deliberately so the case could have a defendant to test the law. The trial was held partially outdoors because the crowd was too large for the courthouse; the judge moved proceedings to the lawn to prevent the floor from collapsing. Scopes was convicted and fined $100, a verdict later thrown out not on constitutional grounds but on a technicality about who had set the fine amount.

events.label: Death of William Jennings Bryan
events.description: William Jennings Bryan, three-time Democratic presidential candidate and the Scopes prosecution's most famous advocate, died in his sleep in Dayton, Tennessee just five days after the trial ended — at 65, having never left the town where he had been publicly humiliated in front of the country.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bryan had diabetes and was already in poor health during the trial; the intense July heat in a non-air-conditioned courtroom and the strain of Darrow's examination almost certainly contributed. His death was read by the urban press as the symbolic end of rural Protestant America, a narrative the modernist press had been building all week; sympathizers in the South and Midwest saw a martyr. He had been working on a speech responding to Darrow the night he died, which was never delivered.

events.label: Aimee Semple McPherson's Angelus Temple
events.description: Evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson opened the 5,300-seat Angelus Temple in Los Angeles in January 1923 and launched KFSG, one of the first religious radio stations in the United States, building a media-and-ministry empire that reached millions — and then became a tabloid sensation in 1926 when she vanished for five weeks and reappeared with a kidnapping story almost no one believed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: McPherson's sermons were theatrical productions with costumes, props, and live orchestras — she called them 'illustrated sermons' and drew sellout crowds even on weeknights. Her KFSG station went on air in February 1924, making her one of the first broadcasters to use radio specifically to build a religious audience and solicit donations over the air. When she disappeared in May 1926, thousands of followers held prayer vigils on the beach in Santa Monica believing she had drowned; when she walked out of the Arizona desert weeks later claiming kidnapping, a grand jury investigation found the evidence so contradictory it could not determine what had actually happened.

events.label: The fundamentalist–modernist controversy
events.description: American Protestantism split through the 1920s between 'modernists,' who wanted to reconcile Christianity with science and modern scholarship, and 'fundamentalists,' who insisted on the literal truth of the Bible and a set of non-negotiable doctrines — a fault line that cracked open nearly every major denomination in the country.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The word 'fundamentalist' comes from a 90-pamphlet series called The Fundamentals, published between 1910 and 1915 and paid for by two wealthy California oilmen; about three million copies were mailed free to ministers, missionaries, and seminarians across the country. The schism was sharpest among Presbyterians, ultimately leading conservative faculty at Princeton Theological Seminary to break off and found the rival Westminster Theological Seminary in 1929. The controversy was not only theological: control of denominational colleges, mission boards, and publishing houses was at stake in every fight.

events.label: The Model T conquers America
events.description: Ford's Model T — the "Tin Lizzie" — made the car a middle-class object for the first time. The price fell from $780 in 1910 to $290 by 1924, and by 1927 Ford had built roughly 15 million of them, making it the bestselling car in history up to that point.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Model T was designed with interchangeable parts so precise that any T could be repaired with parts from any other T — a revolutionary idea when most machines were one-off craftwork. Ford offered it in multiple colors through most of its run; the famous "any color so long as it is black" period only applied during peak-production years when black enamel dried fastest. The car's formal production ended May 26, 1927, after an unbroken 18-year run.

events.label: The legacy of the five-dollar day
events.description: In January 1914 Henry Ford doubled the base wage to five dollars a day and cut the shift to eight hours — then a radical act that other industrialists thought suicidal. The real logic was not generosity but system design: pay your workers enough that they can buy your cars, and you have solved your demand problem.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The announcement drew thousands of men to the Highland Park gates overnight, and Ford had to use fire hoses to disperse the crowd the next morning. The five-dollar day came with strings: Ford's "Sociological Department" inspected workers' homes and habits, and men deemed to be drinking, gambling, or living improperly could be docked back to the old $2.34 rate. Ford's own figures showed turnover at Highland Park had been running several hundred percent annually before the raise — hiring many times the full workforce each year just to keep the line staffed.

events.label: Alfred Sloan reorganizes General Motors
events.description: Alfred Sloan took the helm of General Motors in 1923 and invented modern American corporate marketing: a ladder of brands from Chevrolet to Cadillac, annual styling changes that made last year's car look old, and a finance arm (GMAC) that let customers buy on credit. By 1927 the strategy had beaten Ford's one-cheap-car-forever model decisively.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sloan structured GM not as a single company but as a federation of semi-autonomous divisions (Chevrolet, Pontiac, Oldsmobile, Buick, Cadillac), each with its own management and brand identity but sharing centralized financial controls — a corporate architecture so influential it became the template for the modern conglomerate. His concept of "planned obsolescence" was not about making cars break down; it was about making them look outdated, so customers wanted a new one while the old one still ran perfectly. Sloan ran GM for over three decades and was widely considered the most influential business executive of the twentieth century.

events.label: Ford's Model A changeover
events.description: In May 1927 Ford abruptly stopped making the Model T and shut every plant for six months while 60,000 workers sat idle — the most dramatic industrial changeover in American history. The replacement Model A, introduced in December 1927 as a 1928 model, drew over a million advance orders before a single customer had driven one.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The shutdown cost Ford an estimated $250 million (roughly $4.5 billion today) and permanently ended the company's dominant market position. The new Model A was available in four standard colors — a direct concession to everything Sloan had said about consumer choice — and featured a conventional sliding-gear transmission rather than the T's unique pedal system, which had forced every new driver to learn a completely different technique. Ford's refusal to update the T sooner is studied in business schools as a classic case of a founder's emotional attachment to a product overriding market signals for years.

events.label: Route 66 commissioned
events.description: U.S. Route 66, commissioned November 11, 1926, ran 2,448 miles (3,940 km) from Chicago to Los Angeles — the first continuous paved road connecting the Midwest to the Pacific Coast. It was the spine of the new roadside economy: gas stations, diners, motor courts, and roadside attractions that didn't exist before the car.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Route 66 was the only U.S. numbered highway to be diagonal rather than roughly horizontal or vertical, slicing southwest across seven states and earning the nickname "the Main Street of America." It was fully paved end-to-end only in 1938, more than a decade after commissioning — for much of the twenties significant stretches were still graded dirt. The route became a national symbol of escape and movement during the Great Depression, when hundreds of thousands of displaced Dust Bowl families drove it west toward California, a migration John Steinbeck immortalized by calling it "the mother road" in The Grapes of Wrath (1939).

events.label: Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1921
events.description: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1921 (also called the Phipps Act) put the federal government into road-building for the first time, matching state funds dollar for dollar to build a coherent national highway network. It was the legal and financial foundation for everything the car decade built — suburbs, trucking, roadside commerce, and cross-country travel.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The act was crafted by Thomas Harris MacDonald, head of the National Highway Commission, who would run federal road policy for the next three decades and shaped every major highway bill through the 1950s. It limited federal funds to a "primary system" of roads totaling no more than 7 percent of each state's total road mileage — a deliberate focus on the most important long-distance routes rather than spreading money thin. President Warren Harding signed it on November 9, 1921; within five years the numbered U.S. Route system, including Route 66, was operating on its framework.

events.label: The first car suburbs
events.description: Cheap cars and new paved roads severed the old link between where you lived and where you worked, and the result was the planned, low-density, car-dependent suburb — a new kind of place that did not exist before the automobile. Zoning laws, spreading fast in the twenties, locked the form in permanently by barring shops, apartments, and factories from designated single-family districts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The U.S. Supreme Court upheld local zoning laws as constitutional in Euclid v. Ambler Realty (1926), which gave cities and suburbs the permanent legal power to enforce residential-only zones. Kansas City's Country Club District, developed by J.C. Nichols from the 1910s through the twenties, was the most-studied planned suburb of the era and introduced deed restrictions that explicitly barred Black families from buying — a legal mechanism that spread nationally and helped encode racial segregation into the suburban form itself. By 1930 the U.S. Census recorded suburb growth outpacing city growth for the first time in American history.

events.label: The electrified home
events.description: Between 1918 and the end of the twenties, the share of American homes with electricity jumped from a minority to roughly two-thirds — but almost entirely in cities. Farms were left out almost entirely, a divide that would not close until the Rural Electrification Act of 1936.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The electric refrigerator replaced not just the icebox but an entire daily-delivery industry: the iceman who brought a block of ice to your kitchen every morning effectively disappeared within a decade. Historians of housework have documented a sharp irony in labor-saving appliances: the vacuum cleaner raised the expected standard of cleanliness so much that carpets vacuumed weekly replaced carpets beaten a few times a year, and total domestic labor time did not fall — it was reassigned and intensified. Calvin Coolidge took the presidential oath of office in 1923 by kerosene lamp at his father's Vermont farm, a detail already striking contemporaries as a symbol of how recent and uneven electrification still was.

events.label: The installment-credit economy
events.description: The installment plan turned buying on credit from a mark of poverty into an ordinary middle-class move: take the car or refrigerator home today, pay in fixed monthly amounts with interest, and forfeit it if you miss. By the late twenties, installment debt had become a permanent structural feature of the American economy rather than an emergency.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before the twenties, consumer debt carried a genuine moral stigma rooted in Protestant thrift culture — 'neither a borrower nor a lender be' was a social value, not just a Shakespeare line. The sellers of goods were the ones who deliberately dissolved that stigma, because installment plans expanded their market far beyond cash buyers. GMAC (General Motors Acceptance Corporation), founded in 1919, was one of the first manufacturer-owned finance arms, letting GM sell cars to people who could never have saved up the purchase price.

events.label: The modern advertising industry
events.description: Madison Avenue agencies in the twenties invented the modern ad: not a description of the product but an appeal to fear, status, or desire. The Listerine 'halitosis' campaign is the textbook case — an obscure antiseptic became a mass product by convincing Americans their breath was secretly costing them romance.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ad executive Bruce Barton's 1925 book 'The Man Nobody Knows' became a number-one bestseller by arguing that Jesus of Nazareth was history's greatest advertiser and executive — a man who took twelve obscure fishermen and built an organization that conquered the world. Total U.S. advertising spending roughly doubled between 1919 and 1929, rising to about $3.4 billion a year, making it one of the decade's fastest-growing industries. Radio added a new delivery mechanism mid-decade: the first sponsored broadcast aired in 1922, and by 1929 national brands could speak directly into tens of millions of living rooms.

events.label: The rise of the chain store
events.description: A&P, Woolworth, and Piggly Wiggly expanded to thousands of identical stores in the twenties, buying in bulk volumes that let them undersell any local merchant. Piggly Wiggly's self-service aisle — where the customer picked a labeled package off a shelf themselves — was the moment the brand on the package replaced the word of the clerk.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly in Memphis in 1916 and patented the self-service layout itself, then franchised it nationwide. The number of chain-store outlets in the U.S. grew from roughly 29,000 in 1918 to over 160,000 by 1929. Independent merchants fought back through state legislatures, eventually winning anti-chain-store taxes in dozens of states in the 1930s — a political fight that illustrates exactly how much economic disruption the format caused.

events.label: The radio craze
events.description: Radio exploded from a hobbyist's gadget to a living-room fixture in under a decade: set sales jumped from $60 million in 1922 to $850 million by 1929, and by decade's end roughly a third of American homes had one. Nothing like it had existed before — millions of strangers experiencing the same voice, song, and joke at the exact same moment.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Early radio listeners often built their own crystal sets from kits, and the act of tuning in was itself a novelty — families would gather around to hear distant stations through static. The BBC launched in 1922 as a public, license-fee-funded alternative to America's advertiser-driven model, a structural fork whose consequences shaped both countries' media for the entire century. Radio also ended the phonograph's monopoly on home music and within a few years began eating into theater ticket sales.

events.label: NBC, the first radio network
events.description: In November 1926, RCA (the Radio Corporation of America) launched NBC — the National Broadcasting Company — linking local stations across the country with leased telephone lines so a single program could go out nationwide at once. It was the world's first permanent national radio network, and the commercial logic it established still underlies American broadcasting.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: NBC actually launched as two networks, the Red and Blue, competing with each other to fill different time slots — a quirk that lasted until the government forced it to sell the Blue Network in 1943 (it became ABC). The network model flipped the economics of radio: instead of stations selling local ads, national advertisers could now buy every station at once, which is why entire shows bore sponsor names like 'The Lucky Strike Dance Orchestra.'

events.label: CBS founded
events.description: CBS (the Columbia Broadcasting System) launched in 1927 and was bought the following year by 26-year-old William S. Paley, a cigar heir from Philadelphia who turned a small struggling network into NBC's great rival. Two national networks, both advertiser-funded, now competed for the same mass audience.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Paley's key insight was locking affiliate stations into the network by paying them, where NBC charged affiliates for programming — an aggressive move that flipped dozens of stations to CBS. He would run the network for six decades, eventually building the news division that gave the country Edward R. Murrow and Walter Cronkite. The building CBS still occupies in New York, known as Black Rock, was designed by Eero Saarinen in 1965.

events.label: Radio Act of 1927
events.description: By the mid-1920s hundreds of radio stations were broadcasting on overlapping frequencies, turning the airwaves into a cacophonous mess. The Radio Act of 1927 created the Federal Radio Commission to license stations in 'the public interest' and established the foundational American principle that the electromagnetic spectrum is public property.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Act replaced a 1912 law written when radio meant ship-to-shore Morse code, long before anyone imagined broadcasting. It gave the new commission power to revoke licenses — a real threat that pushed commercial stations to behave. The 1927 framework was itself superseded by the Communications Act of 1934, which created the FCC (Federal Communications Commission) that still regulates American broadcast media today.

events.label: The Hollywood studio system
events.description: By the early 1920s a handful of large studios — many founded by Eastern European Jewish immigrants who had been locked out of older American industries — controlled movies from the script to the ticket window, owning production lots, distribution networks, and the theaters themselves. This integrated model made movies the country's fourth-largest industry.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The studio system's power rested on 'block booking,' a practice that forced theater owners to buy packages of films sight-unseen rather than pick individual titles — if you wanted the hit, you took the whole slate. Major studios also kept actors, directors, and writers on long-term exclusive contracts, meaning a star's career, image, and roles were entirely controlled by the studio. The Supreme Court broke up the system in 1948, ruling that owning both studios and theaters was an illegal monopoly.

events.label: The Fatty Arbuckle scandal
events.description: Roscoe 'Fatty' Arbuckle was one of silent Hollywood's biggest stars — at his peak earning $1 million a year from Paramount — when a woman died after a party in his San Francisco hotel room in September 1921. Three trials followed; the third jury acquitted him and issued a written apology, but his career was destroyed before the verdict.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Arbuckle had mentored both Buster Keaton and Charlie Chaplin and was considered one of the most gifted physical comedians alive at the time of his arrest. The press, led by William Randolph Hearst's papers, covered the case as if the verdict were already in — providing a textbook early example of tabloid media manufacturing a conviction. Arbuckle eventually returned to directing under a pseudonym but never recovered his star status; he died in 1933.

events.label: The Hays Office
events.description: Spooked by the Arbuckle scandal and a cluster of other Hollywood controversies, the studios hired former Postmaster General Will Hays in 1922 to run a self-censorship office — a preemptive move to ward off government regulation. Hays's office eventually produced the Production Code, a detailed list of forbidden content that governed American films from 1934 until the late 1960s.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Production Code banned, among other things, any 'lustful' kissing, depicting drug trafficking, and showing a crime in a way that might inspire imitation. It also forbade portraying interracial romance — a racial restriction baked into the industry's self-policing from the beginning. Studio heads discovered the Code had a useful side effect: foreign markets with stricter censorship were easier to enter with pre-sanitized films, so compliance also opened export revenue.

events.label: Rudolph Valentino, the first heartthrob
events.description: Rudolph Valentino — born Rodolfo Guglielmi in southern Italy — became the silent screen's defining romantic idol, particularly after The Sheik (1921) made him a household name. When he died suddenly of peritonitis in August 1926 at 31, an estimated 100,000 people lined up outside the New York funeral home, and the press reported riots and fan suicides.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Valentino's exotic, overtly sensual screen persona made some male critics uneasy — a Chicago newspaper column mocked him as a 'pink powder puff,' an attack on what they saw as foreign-corrupted American masculinity. His death triggered what may have been the first modern mass-media grief event: the fan response to a stranger known only through film. Eight biographies were published within a year of his death, and his estate remained contested for decades.

events.label: Chaplin's The Gold Rush
events.description: Charlie Chaplin's The Gold Rush (1925), with the boot-eating dinner and the dance of the rolls, was the silent era's comic peak and a global success. Chaplin's Tramp was arguably the most recognized human image on earth in the twenties.

events.label: The Jazz Singer and sound film
events.description: Warner Bros.' The Jazz Singer, which opened on October 6, 1927, was the first feature film to carry synchronized singing and dialogue, using the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system. It killed the silent era within three years — and its headline performance was Al Jolson in blackface, the minstrel tradition delivered on the new medium to the whole country at once.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The silent film it displaced had been a genuinely international art form: a Chaplin short required no translation and played identically in Paris, Tokyo, or Buenos Aires. Sound shattered that universality overnight — foreign stars with thick accents lost their careers, and foreign markets suddenly needed dubbed or subtitled prints. Warner Bros. took the sound risk partly because they were the weakest of the major studios and needed a gamble; the bet made them a major player.

events.label: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
events.description: Founded in 1927, the Academy was created partly to head off Hollywood unionization and burnish the industry's prestige. Its awards, first given in 1929, became the movie business's self-coronation.

events.label: The tabloid press
events.description: The New York Daily News (1919) and its imitators built mass circulation on photographs, crime, sex, and sport. The 1928 secret photograph of Ruth Snyder's execution and the Hall–Mills murder trial defined the tabloid's appetite for sensation.

events.label: Babe Ruth and the home-run era
events.description: Babe Ruth's 60 home runs in 1927 — a record that stood for 34 years — capped a career that remade baseball into a power spectacle and turned him into the closest thing to a globally famous athlete the world had yet seen, earning him nicknames 'the Bambino' and 'the Sultan of Swat.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ruth began his career as a genuinely elite left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox before the Yankees converted him to an outfielder full-time, a position switch nearly without precedent for someone of his pitching caliber. The Red Sox sold his contract to the Yankees in 1920 for $100,000 — the famous 'Curse of the Bambino' that Boston fans blamed for the team's 86-year World Series drought. He was among the first five players elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame when it opened in 1936.

events.label: The 'Long Count' fight
events.description: The September 1927 'Long Count' fight in Chicago — Gene Tunney versus Jack Dempsey before 104,000 fans — became the decade's defining sports controversy: a delayed count let Tunney recover from a seventh-round knockdown and keep his heavyweight title, while the gate surpassed $2 million.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'long count' controversy arose because Illinois rules required a knocked-down fighter's opponent to retreat to a neutral corner before the count began — Dempsey hesitated, costing Tunney roughly five extra seconds on the canvas. Radio broadcasts brought the fight to an estimated 50 million listeners, the largest radio audience for a single event in American history to that point. Tunney retired undefeated as champion the following year, one of the few champions ever to do so.

events.label: Red Grange turns pro
events.description: Illinois halfback 'Red' Grange, the Galloping Ghost, signed with the Chicago Bears days after his last college game in 1925, drawing 70,000 fans and putting the struggling National Football League on the map.

events.label: Bobby Jones and the golf boom
events.description: Amateur Bobby Jones dominated golf in the twenties, winning thirteen majors and, in 1930, the Grand Slam. Mass-market golf and the country club spread with the suburbs and the new leisure economy.

events.label: Gertrude Ederle swims the Channel
events.description: On August 6, 1926, twenty-year-old Gertrude Ederle became the first woman to swim the English Channel, crossing in 14 hours and 31 minutes — nearly two hours faster than any man had done it — and returned to a New York ticker-tape parade that proved a woman could be a national sports hero.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ederle had already won a gold medal at the 1924 Paris Olympics as part of the U.S. relay team, and held world records in five swimming events before her Channel attempt. She crossed using a freestyle (crawl) stroke, while the men whose records she beat had used the slower breaststroke — a technical advantage the press sometimes downplayed. The press had nicknamed her 'Queen of the Waves,' and her Channel crossing generated more newspaper front pages than any athletic feat by a woman up to that point.

events.label: Lindbergh's solo Atlantic flight
events.description: On May 20–21, 1927, twenty-five-year-old airmail pilot Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris — 3,600 miles (5,800 km) in 33.5 hours — the first solo nonstop transatlantic crossing and the most celebrated aviation feat in history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lindbergh competed for the $25,000 Orteig Prize, offered since 1919 for the first nonstop New York-to-Paris crossing; six people had already died attempting it. He had no radio, used a periscope to see forward because a fuel tank blocked the cockpit windshield, and stayed awake the entire flight by sticking his hand out the window into the cold air. The flight set a world distance record for a nonstop flight by nearly 2,000 miles (3,200 km).

events.label: The aviation boom
events.description: Lindbergh's flight set off an 'aviation craze': stock in aircraft companies soared, airmail contracts created the first airlines, and Congress poured money into airports. Aviation became both a real industry and a speculative mania.

events.label: Amelia Earhart crosses the Atlantic
events.description: Amelia Earhart became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air in 1928, as a passenger, and was instantly made a celebrity by publisher George Putnam. She used the fame to campaign for women in aviation and to plan her own solo flights.

events.label: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five recordings
events.description: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recording sessions (1925–28) produced some of the most influential records in American music — small studio groups in which Armstrong's trumpet solos pulled the individual voice out from the collective jazz front line and made it the center of the form.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Armstrong grew up in New Orleans, learned cornet in a reform school, and was mentored by King Oliver before moving to Chicago. His nickname 'Satchmo' (short for 'Satchel Mouth') followed him for life. The Hot Five recordings were never performed live in that configuration — they were assembled purely for the studio, which is part of why they sound so focused; there was no crowd to play to, only the microphone.

events.label: Duke Ellington at the Cotton Club
events.description: Duke Ellington's orchestra began its residency at Harlem's Cotton Club in December 1927, and the club's nightly radio broadcasts made him a household name across the country — fame earned performing for a whites-only audience that excluded the Harlem community he was performing in.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ellington composed specifically for the Cotton Club's 'jungle'-themed stage shows, writing music meant to evoke an exoticized Africa for white audiences — a creative constraint he turned into genuine innovation in texture and tone. Music critic Ralph J. Gleason later called him 'America's most important composer,' a judgment that credits work that began in those compromised circumstances.

events.label: Bessie Smith, 'Empress of the Blues'
events.description: Bessie Smith's 1923 debut recording sold 800,000 copies in its first year and made her the highest-paid Black entertainer of the decade, earning her the title 'Empress of the Blues' — her voice carried Southern Black music through the phonograph to a national audience.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Smith's records were sold as 'race records' — an industry term for recordings marketed specifically to Black buyers, kept on a separate catalog from mainstream releases. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989. Despite her commercial dominance, she died in 1937 after a car accident in Mississippi, and her grave went unmarked for over thirty years until Janis Joplin and a Philadelphia club owner paid for a headstone.

events.label: Jelly Roll Morton and recorded jazz
events.description: Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers recordings (1926–27) were among the first to fully arrange jazz, fixing the New Orleans style on record. The phonograph and radio were spreading a regional Black music nationwide within a few years.

events.label: Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue
events.description: George Gershwin premiered Rhapsody in Blue in New York in February 1924, an attempt to fuse jazz with the concert hall. It signaled jazz crossing into mainstream and 'respectable' American music.

events.label: Locke's The New Negro
events.description: Alain Locke's 1925 anthology The New Negro — gathering Hughes, Hurston, McKay, Toomer, and others — became the defining text of the Harlem Renaissance, arguing that a new generation of urban Black Americans was remaking American culture from Harlem outward.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Locke was the first Black American Rhodes Scholar and a Howard University philosophy professor; his connections and taste made him the movement's de facto impresario. The anthology's first section, 'The Negro Renaissance,' included poetry, fiction, and essays all arguing the same claim: Black artists should stop asking for white approval and start making their own standards.

events.label: Langston Hughes, The Weary Blues
events.description: Langston Hughes published The Weary Blues in 1926 and his essay 'The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain' the same year, insisting that Black writers should draw on jazz, blues, and vernacular speech rather than imitate white literary models — the manifesto of a generation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hughes was born in Joplin, Missouri, and is credited as an early inventor of jazz poetry, a form that built the rhythms of live jazz directly into printed verse. He supported himself in New York partly by working as a busboy before Lincoln Center-era fame; his first book was accepted after a chance encounter in a hotel restaurant when he slipped poems next to the plate of the poet Vachel Lindsay.

events.label: Zora Neale Hurston in Harlem
events.description: Zora Neale Hurston arrived in Harlem in 1925 with training as an anthropologist under Franz Boas and spent the decade collecting Southern Black folklore, ghost tales, and work songs before anyone else thought to write them down.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Her four novels, more than fifty short stories, an autobiography, and several ethnographies ranged from the American South to Haiti and Jamaica; her 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God is now her best-known work but was largely forgotten for decades after her death. Her fieldwork used ethnomusicological methods to study communities of color respectfully, long before formal academic boundaries for that discipline existed.

events.label: Claude McKay's protest verse
events.description: Jamaican-born Claude McKay gave the Harlem Renaissance its angriest early voice — his 1919 sonnet 'If We Must Die,' written in the heat of the Red Summer, and his 1922 collection Harlem Shadows established him as the movement's militant conscience.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: McKay was a central figure in the Harlem Renaissance despite spending much of the decade in London, Moscow, and Paris; his 1928 novel Home to Harlem became a bestseller, though some peers, including W.E.B. Du Bois, found its frank depiction of Harlem nightlife too raw. 'If We Must Die' was later quoted by Winston Churchill in a wartime speech, though Churchill never named McKay as the author.

events.label: The Cotton Club
events.description: The Cotton Club opened in Harlem in 1923 under bootlegger Owney Madden, became the most famous nightclub in America, presented the greatest Black musical talent of the age in 'jungle'-themed revues — and by strict policy admitted only white customers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The club ran at 142nd Street and Lenox Avenue until 1936, then briefly in the midtown theater district until 1940; its roster reads like a who's-who of the Jazz Age: Ellington, Armstrong, Cab Calloway, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday, the Nicholas Brothers. Performers entered through the service entrance; the same artists could not buy a ticket to watch each other perform from the audience.

events.label: The NAACP anti-lynching campaign
events.description: The NAACP drove the Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill through the House of Representatives in 1922, only to watch Southern senators kill it with a filibuster — a procedural move where a senator holds the floor indefinitely, blocking a vote unless a supermajority forces debate to end.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The bill's sponsor, Republican Leonidas Dyer of Missouri, had introduced it first in 1918 after witnessing the East St. Louis massacre in his district. The Senate filibuster that killed it in 1922 was led by Southern Democrats who openly stated they were protecting the practice; the same tactic would be deployed against every federal anti-lynching measure for the next four decades.

events.label: A. Philip Randolph and the Pullman porters
events.description: A.
