Philip Randolph founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925, organizing the Black men who staffed Pullman railroad sleeping cars — the largest single employer of Black men in America — into the first Black-led union to win a charter in the American Federation of Labor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The union took twelve years to win its first contract with the Pullman Company (signed 1937), making it one of the longest labor campaigns in American history. Randolph's porters were also one of the main distribution networks for the Black press: because they traveled the whole country, they carried copies of the Chicago Defender and other papers south into communities where white authorities had banned the publications.

events.label: Garvey convicted and deported
events.description: In 1923 Marcus Garvey was convicted of mail fraud tied to his Black Star steamship line, sentenced to five years, and deported to Jamaica in 1927 — ending the largest Black mass organization in American history and a long controversy over whether the prosecution was politically motivated.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: J. Edgar Hoover, then head of the FBI's predecessor Bureau of Investigation, had been trying to deport Garvey since 1919 and personally assigned agents to build the fraud case. Many of Garvey's supporters and later historians argued the prosecution was a political hit to destroy the movement rather than a genuine financial crime, and the controversy has never fully settled.

events.label: Fitzgerald's This Side of Paradise
events.description: F. Scott Fitzgerald's debut novel This Side of Paradise (1920) launched him to fame at 23, portraying the carefree, morally adrift youth of the new Jazz Age through Princeton student Amory Blaine's unfulfilling romances and literary dabbling.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Fitzgerald took the title from a line in Rupert Brooke's poem 'Tiare Tahiti,' not from his own imagination. Charles Scribner's Sons accepted the manuscript after years of Fitzgerald revising it — the book had been rejected multiple times before landing its publisher. The novel's frank treatment of young women and romance was considered bold enough in 1920 that many libraries refused to stock it.

events.label: The Great Gatsby published
events.description: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925) translated the decade's bootleg wealth, lavish parties, and moral emptiness into a single story — Jay Gatsby's doomed obsession with the unattainable Daisy Buchanan — and became the novel by which the whole era is now understood.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The book sold only around 20,000 copies in its first year, a disappointment that haunted Fitzgerald for the rest of his life; he died in 1940 believing it a failure. It was a military printing during World War II — cheap paperback editions distributed to soldiers — that began its second life as a classic. Fitzgerald set the novel on Long Island's 'Gold Coast,' directly inspired by the lavish mansions he could see but could not afford while living in Great Neck.

events.label: Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises
events.description: Ernest Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926) gave the disillusioned postwar generation its defining portrait — expatriates drinking, watching bullfights, and failing to connect — and introduced the iceberg prose style, plain and declarative, that transformed American fiction.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: When it was published in October 1926, reviews were decidedly mixed: many critics found the characters dissolute and unsympathetic, and some were offended by its frank treatment of sexuality and alcohol. Jonathan Cape published it in Britain the following year under the title Fiesta. Hemingway biographer Jeffrey Meyers later called it Hemingway's greatest work — a judgment that would have surprised the contemporary reviewers who dismissed it.

events.label: The Lost Generation in Paris
events.description: The 'Lost Generation' — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Ezra Pound, and others — congregated in 1920s Paris, drawn by a strong dollar, light censorship, and legal wine, and produced much of the defining literature of the twentieth century from Gertrude Stein's salon and Sylvia Beach's bookshop.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gertrude Stein coined 'Lost Generation' by adapting a remark her garage owner made about young mechanics who had no discipline — she applied it to the postwar youth who seemed similarly adrift. Hemingway later said he doubted the label was true, calling it 'splendid bombast.' The dollar's strength in France was staggering: an American writer could live comfortably in Paris on what was considered a modest income back home.

events.label: H. L. Mencken and The American Mercury
events.description: Baltimore critic H. L. Mencken co-founded The American Mercury in 1924 and spent the decade as the most quoted American writer — a relentless satirist of Prohibition, the Klan, fundamentalism, and the smug conformist middle class he called the 'booboisie.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mencken coined or popularized so many terms that 'Menckenian' entered multiple dictionaries to describe his combative rhetorical style. His coinage 'the Bible Belt' for the evangelical South came directly from his coverage of the Scopes Trial, which he dubbed 'the Monkey Trial' — the nickname that stuck. At his peak in the mid-1920s, The American Mercury sold over 77,000 copies a month, a remarkable circulation for a literary-political magazine.

events.label: The Algonquin Round Table
events.description: Dorothy Parker, Robert Benchley, and a circle of New York wits lunched daily at the Algonquin Hotel through the early twenties, their quips amplified by newspaper columns. They embodied the decade's urbane, sardonic literary celebrity.

events.label: The flapper and the 'New Woman'
events.description: The 'flapper' — bobbed hair, knee-length skirts, cosmetics in public, cigarettes, cocktails — became the decade's image of liberated young womanhood, a genuine cultural revolt against Victorian constraint that was also, simultaneously, a media and advertising construction.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Flappers gained unexpected freedom of movement through the spread of the automobile, which offered privacy and independence unavailable to earlier generations of young women. The style spread internationally, with versions appearing in Britain, France, and beyond, though the American flapper became the global archetype through Hollywood films. The word itself predates the 1920s — it had been British slang for an immature young woman since at least the 1890s — but acquired its new meaning and global currency in the postwar decade.

events.label: The Charleston
events.description: The Charleston exploded out of the 1923 Broadway musical Runnin' Wild — composed by James P. Johnson — and became the decade's defining dance craze, its frantic kicks and swinging arms a full-body rejection of Victorian propriety.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Charleston took its name from the harbor city of Charleston, South Carolina, where the rhythm had roots in the Gullah communities of the Carolina Lowcountry. Its peak popularity actually came in 1926–1927, slightly after the Runnin' Wild premiere, as it spread from Black dance halls to white ballrooms to Hollywood films. The dance was so energetic that some venues banned it after a 1925 balcony collapse in Boston was blamed (unfairly) on Charleston dancers.

events.label: Speakeasies and bootlegging
events.description: A speakeasy — slang for an illegal bar where you'd 'speak easy' (quietly) at the door to get a password entry — replaced the saloon under Prohibition and multiplied wildly. New York City alone may have had 30,000 or more operating at peak, more drinking establishments than had existed before the ban.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name 'speakeasy' predates Prohibition, appearing in the 1880s to describe bars that sold without a license. Unlike the often-squalid pre-Prohibition saloon, many speakeasies admitted women and mixed social classes, inadvertently accelerating the gender-mixing of American nightlife. Some of the most famous, like New York's '21' Club, had elaborate hidden wine cellars with shelving that could be tilted to send bottles sliding into a sealed vault during raids.

events.label: Rum Row and the bootleg supply chain
events.description: Bootleggers (smugglers of illegal alcohol) built an entire supply chain to keep speakeasies stocked: foreign ships anchored on 'Rum Row' just outside U.S. territorial waters while fast motorboats dashed the liquor ashore, and gangs like Detroit's Purple Gang ran Canadian whiskey across the river by boat and car.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The federal government's attempt to fight bootlegging created an unintended side effect: to stop bootleggers from repurposing industrial alcohol (legally made for solvents and fuel), authorities ordered it 'denatured' — deliberately laced with methanol and other poisons. Bootleggers redistilled it imperfectly, and the resulting deaths from tainted liquor numbered in the thousands, a fact the government was fully aware of. The high-speed souped-up cars built to outrun agents on back roads fed directly into the Southern bootleg-car culture that seeded NASCAR.

events.label: Prohibition and organized crime
events.description: Prohibition transformed American criminal gangs from small local rackets into large, business-like organizations with manufacturing, distribution, and systematic bribery of police and politicians. The modern American Mafia — the Cosa Nostra crime syndicates that would dominate organized crime for decades — was built on the infrastructure and profits of twenties bootlegging.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The American Mafia's organizational structure — distinct crime 'families' each controlling a city or region — solidified during Prohibition, when the need to divide bootlegging territories forced rival gangs to negotiate and formalize boundaries. When Prohibition ended in 1933, the organizations didn't dissolve; they simply pivoted into gambling, labor racketeering, and narcotics, carrying the same bribery networks and enforcement methods intact.

events.label: Al Capone runs Chicago
events.description: Al Capone, nicknamed 'Scarface,' took over the Chicago Outfit crime syndicate in 1925 and ran it until 1931 — building a bootlegging, gambling, and vice empire that reportedly grossed around $60 million a year while he openly cultivated a celebrity image, gave press interviews, and sat in box seats at baseball games.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Capone was finally brought down not for murder or bootlegging but for federal income-tax evasion — convicted in 1931 and sentenced to 11 years. He was just 33 years old when imprisoned. After release he lived out his days in declining health from syphilis, dying in 1947 at 48, having never returned to power. The IRS's successful prosecution of Capone made 'following the money' through tax records a permanent tool of organized-crime investigation.

events.label: St. Valentine's Day Massacre
events.description: On February 14, 1929, Capone gunmen — some disguised in police uniforms — lined up seven members of Bugs Moran's rival North Side Gang against a garage wall on Chicago's North Clark Street and machine-gunned them. The massacre shocked the public less with its body count than with the realization that the killers had impersonated police.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Despite being widely attributed to Capone, no one was ever convicted for the St. Valentine's Day Massacre. The disguise tactic — fake cop uniforms — was what turned public opinion; it wasn't just gang violence but a deliberate mockery of law enforcement. Capone himself was in Florida at the time, giving him an alibi that investigators could never disprove.

events.label: Prohibition's failure becomes undeniable
events.description: By the mid-twenties poisoned industrial alcohol was killing thousands, the government was deliberately denaturing it, juries refused to convict, and 'wet' politics was rising. Prohibition's collapse was visible years before its 1933 repeal.

events.label: 'The business of America is business'
events.description: In a January 1925 speech to newspaper editors, Coolidge declared that 'the chief business of the American people is business' — almost always misquoted as simply 'the business of America is business.' The line became the decade's defining political motto, shorthand for an administration that cut taxes and kept the government out of the economy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The full speech was more nuanced than the famous fragment; Coolidge also praised journalism, education, and religion as essential pursuits. His Revenue Act of 1926 cut the top income-tax rate to 24 percent, down from 73 percent at the start of the decade. Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon — already one of the wealthiest men in America — was the architect of the cuts and believed lower rates on the rich would eventually benefit everyone, a doctrine later labeled 'trickle-down.'

events.label: The 1926 Revenue Act
events.description: The Revenue Act of 1926 slashed the top income-tax rate to 25 percent, eliminated the gift tax, gutted the estate tax, and ended public access to federal income-tax returns — the centerpiece of Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon's decade-long campaign to cut taxes on wealth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Act also reduced taxes in lower brackets and cancelled a range of excise taxes on goods. Federal revenues actually held up through the boom years, which Mellon and Coolidge cited as proof that lower rates paid for themselves. The estate-tax gutting was particularly controversial: critics argued it permanently entrenched the era's fortunes and was a gift to families like Mellon's own.

events.label: The farm depression of the twenties
events.description: American farmers, close to a third of the country's population, had borrowed heavily to expand during WWI's price surge; when demand collapsed after 1919, prices never recovered and roughly a quarter of farmers lost their land through the decade. The rural depression the 1930s made famous was already running in full by the mid-1920s.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The McNary–Haugen bill, co-authored by two Republican congressmen, proposed that the government buy surplus crops at a high domestic price and dump them abroad at a loss to keep American farm prices stable — a mechanism its opponents called price-fixing. Coolidge vetoed it twice, in 1927 and 1928, calling it unconstitutional and economically unsound. The bill had supporters as unlikely as Vice President Charles Dawes, putting Coolidge at odds with his own administration.

events.label: The 'sick industries'
events.description: While cities boomed, coal, textiles, and New England manufacturing stagnated or shrank as cheaper alternatives took their markets: oil displaced coal, Southern mills undercut New England factories, and synthetic fibers ate into cotton and wool. These 'sick industries' employed millions who never saw the decade's prosperity.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 1929 Loray Mill strike in Gastonia, North Carolina — where workers earned as little as $9 a week for 12-hour days — became a national flashpoint; the mill's superintendent was shot dead and the strike's organizer, a Communist union activist, was convicted of murder. Though the strike failed in its immediate goals, historians credit it with galvanizing the broader Southern labor movement. By the late 1920s, the U.S. coal industry employed roughly a third fewer miners than it had in 1920.

events.label: Taylorism and the efficiency cult
events.description: Frederick Taylor's 'scientific management' — the stopwatch, the time-and-motion study, the one-best-way to do any task — had been a factory method since the 1900s, but in the twenties it spread into offices, schools, and homes as 'efficiency' became a national ideology.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Taylor's original system broke every job into its smallest components, timed each with a stopwatch, eliminated wasted motion, and paid workers piece-rates for hitting the optimized speed — a method his critics called 'the systematic soldiering of the worker's body.' By the twenties, home economists were applying Taylorist principles to kitchen layout and cooking sequences, and popular magazines ran efficiency guides for housewives. Henry Ford's assembly line was itself a direct application of Taylorist decomposition of labor, which is why the mass-production chapter and this one are inseparable.

events.label: Freud's American vogue
events.description: Popularized (and simplified) psychoanalysis swept twenties America: the 'inferiority complex,' the unconscious, and 'repression' entered everyday speech and advertising. Edward Bernays applied his uncle Freud's ideas to selling and called it public relations.

events.label: Eugenics and Buck v. Bell
events.description: Eugenics — the belief, endorsed by mainstream science, that human worth was heritable and the state should breed 'better' people — was the intellectual framework behind the 1924 immigration quotas. In Buck v. Bell (1927) the Supreme Court blessed forced sterilization with Oliver Wendell Holmes writing: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Carrie Buck, the young Virginia woman whose sterilization the Court upheld, almost certainly was not intellectually disabled — later research suggests she was a normal girl who had been raped by a nephew of her foster family and institutionalized partly to hide the pregnancy. The Buck v. Bell ruling has never been formally overturned; roughly 60,000 Americans were forcibly sterilized under similar laws across the century, with the rate accelerating after the 1927 decision. American eugenicists corresponded with and directly inspired German racial scientists in the 1920s and 1930s — the connection was noted with admiration in Nazi Germany before the U.S. grew uncomfortable with the association after 1945.

events.label: The Butler Act
events.description: Tennessee's Butler Act, signed into law in March 1925, made it a criminal offense for any public school teacher to present a theory that humans evolved from earlier animals rather than the Genesis account of creation — the first such law in the United States and the statute under which Scopes was prosecuted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The act was introduced by John Washington Butler, a farmer and state legislator who had never attended high school himself and was reportedly motivated by a neighbor telling him her daughter had come home from college having learned evolution and lost her faith. The penalty was just a $100 fine for a first offense, which is part of why the ACLU found it easy to recruit a volunteer defendant. Tennessee's law remained on the books for 42 years, finally repealed in 1967.

events.label: Darrow cross-examines Bryan
events.description: On the trial's seventh day, defense attorney Clarence Darrow called prosecutor William Jennings Bryan to the stand as an expert witness on the Bible — an extraordinary procedural gambit Bryan accepted out of vanity — and in front of the national radio audience pressed him on whether Genesis was literally true in every detail, exposing contradictions that the urban press immediately turned into the definitive image of the trial.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bryan had not studied the Bible as a scientific document and was caught off guard by specific questions: could he say how long the six days of creation were, where Cain found his wife, whether Joshua literally made the sun stand still? He admitted under pressure that the 'days' in Genesis might be 'periods' rather than 24-hour days — a concession fundamentalists found damaging. Darrow's actual legal goal was not to win this argument but to get Bryan's testimony into the record to appeal to the Supreme Court, a case that never materialized after Bryan died.

events.label: Billy Sunday's revival circuit
events.description: Former baseball player Billy Sunday was the most famous revivalist of the era, preaching a muscular, anti-modern, pro-Prohibition Christianity to millions in purpose-built wooden tabernacles. He embodied the populist Protestant resistance to the Jazz Age.

events.label: The Florida land boom
events.description: From 1923 to 1925, a land frenzy swept Florida — lots in Miami and the new suburb of Coral Gables were bought sight-unseen with tiny 'binder' down payments and flipped within weeks at a profit, floating entirely on the belief that prices would rise forever.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Florida boom was fueled partly by new infrastructure: the construction of highways and railways made South Florida feel suddenly accessible to northern buyers who had never set foot there. At the mania's peak in 1925, Miami had more real-estate agents than voters. The bust arrived before the hurricane — prices had already started cracking in 1926 when the railroad companies, overwhelmed by freight, imposed embargoes on non-essential shipments into the state, cutting off building materials and stranding the whole speculative chain.

events.label: The 1926 Miami hurricane
events.description: The Great Miami Hurricane of September 1926 killed hundreds and physically demolished the city's booming neighborhoods, delivering the killing blow to Florida's already-deflating land speculation and sending the money north to Wall Street.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The storm hit as a Category 4 with winds above 130 mph, and many Miami residents ran outside after the eye passed — mistaking the calm for the storm's end — only to be caught by the back wall. The $100 million in damage (roughly $1.8 billion today) was a scale of destruction the state would not see again for decades. Because Florida's overextended banks had lent heavily on inflated land values, the hurricane effectively started an early regional depression in Florida four years before the rest of the country felt it.

events.label: Great Mississippi Flood of 1927
events.description: The 1927 Mississippi flood inundated 27,000 square miles, displaced over 600,000 people, and fell hardest on Black sharecroppers conscripted into the levee work. Commerce Secretary Herbert Hoover's relief role helped make him president.

events.label: The skyscraper race
events.description: New developers competed to build the world's tallest building as a corporate billboard. The contest between the Bank of Manhattan at 40 Wall Street, the Chrysler Building, and the planned Empire State Building defined the late-twenties skyline.

events.label: The Chrysler Building rises
events.description: Begun in 1928, the Art Deco Chrysler Building briefly became the world's tallest in 1930 by secretly assembling a 185-foot spire inside the dome and raising it in 90 minutes to beat 40 Wall Street. It is the decade's signature building.

events.label: Art Deco in America
events.description: The streamlined, geometric Art Deco style, launched at a 1925 Paris exposition, swept American skyscrapers, theaters, radios, and cars. It was the visual signature of the machine-age, consumer-age decade.

events.label: The movie palaces
events.description: The 1920s were the golden age of the movie palace — enormous, ornately decorated theaters seating thousands under marble lobbies and gilded ceilings, designed to make a working-class ticket buyer feel like royalty for two hours. The Roxy in New York, which opened in 1927, seated 5,920 and cost $12 million to build.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Movie palace architects often worked in a fantasy-historical style called 'atmospheric': the auditorium ceiling was painted and lit to look like an outdoor night sky, with projected clouds drifting across simulated stars. These theaters typically employed full orchestras, organists, and live stage acts before the feature — a moviegoing experience nothing like the multiplex. Most were demolished in the 1950s–70s as TV killed attendance; the handful that survive are now registered historic landmarks.

events.label: The stadium-building boom
events.description: Yankee Stadium (1923), Soldier Field (1924), the Rose Bowl (1922), and dozens of college stadiums were built as concrete monuments to the new mass spectator sport. Sport became architecture and big business in the same decade.

events.label: Al Smith and anti-Catholicism
events.description: New York Governor Al Smith became the first Catholic nominated for president by a major American party in 1928, and the campaign against him immediately turned into a referendum on whether a Catholic could be trusted to govern independently of the Pope.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Smith's Catholicism was only part of what made him a cultural lightning rod: he was also a wet (anti-Prohibition), a Tammany Hall product, and spoke with a thick Lower East Side accent that rural Protestant voters found alien. Opponents distributed pamphlets claiming the Pope was preparing to move to Washington. Smith actually won some unexpected support in cities, running ahead of the national Democratic ticket there — foreshadowing the urban coalition Franklin Roosevelt would assemble four years later.

events.label: Herbert Hoover elected
events.description: Herbert Hoover, the celebrated engineer who had organized wartime food relief and modernized the Commerce Department, won the 1928 election in a landslide on the promise that American prosperity was permanent and poverty nearly conquered.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hoover carried 40 of 48 states and cracked the old Solid South, winning Florida, Texas, Virginia, and North Carolina in part because of anti-Catholic sentiment against Smith. His acceptance speech that summer contained the line that Americans were 'nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land' — a statement so specific and so soon falsified that it became one of the most-quoted political miscalculations in American history. He took office in March 1929; the crash came seven months later.

events.label: The great bull market
events.description: Stock prices roughly doubled between early 1928 and September 1929, powered by borrowed money, a flood of first-time amateur investors, and the nearly universal belief that the boom was a permanent new state of the world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'Everybody Ought to Be Rich' article was written by John J. Raskob, then chairman of the Democratic Party and a General Motors executive, published in the Ladies' Home Journal in August 1929 — just weeks before the peak. He calculated that $15 a month invested in good stocks would compound to $80,000 in 20 years. The article was cited for decades as the perfect marker of peak euphoria: serious financial advice, in a women's magazine, two months before the collapse.

events.label: Buying on margin
events.description: Buying 'on margin' meant putting down as little as 10 percent in cash and borrowing the rest from your broker, with the stock itself as collateral — a mechanism that multiplied gains spectacularly on the way up and triggered forced, cascading selling on the way down.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At the 1929 peak, brokers' loans to margin buyers totaled roughly $8.5 billion — more than the entire federal budget at the time. The structure was brutal in reverse: if your stock dropped even slightly, the broker issued a 'margin call' demanding immediate cash; if you couldn't pay, he sold your shares at whatever price he could get, which pushed prices down further, triggering the next margin call. This is exactly why the decline accelerated rather than plateaued: every falling price mechanically generated more forced selling.

events.label: Investment trusts and leverage
events.description: Investment trusts — companies whose only business was owning shares in other companies, often themselves purchased on borrowed money, sometimes owning yet other trusts — mushroomed in 1928–29, building towers of leverage that could only collapse faster than anything beneath them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By 1929 there were hundreds of investment trusts, many formed and marketed to the public within months of each other. The Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation, launched in late 1928, grew to a valuation of over $500 million; its shares were eventually worth a few dollars. The layering was the problem: one dollar of real assets might underpin five dollars of trust shares, which were themselves used as collateral for more borrowing, so a 10 percent decline in underlying assets could wipe out 100 percent of the equity at the top of the stack.

events.label: The Federal Reserve and the bubble
events.description: The Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, watched speculation balloon through 1928–29 and could not resolve its core dilemma: raising interest rates would choke the stock speculators but would also strangle the farming and manufacturing sectors that were already struggling.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Fed's indecision was structural as well as political: the twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks and the Washington-based Federal Reserve Board disagreed sharply about whether to act, with New York's Fed pushing for rate hikes and the Board resisting. The Fed did raise rates in 1928 and again in 1929, but too modestly and too late to deflate the bubble without crashing everything else. The deeper failure came after the crash: from 1930 to 1933 the Fed allowed the money supply to contract by roughly a third as thousands of banks failed, which Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz later argued turned a bad crash into the Great Depression.

events.label: The market peaks
events.description: The Dow Jones Industrial Average — a running score of 30 large company stocks used as a thermometer for the whole market — hit its 1920s high of 381 on September 3, 1929, then drifted nervously downward for seven weeks while almost everyone called it a routine correction.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Dow had been at around 191 just eighteen months earlier, in January 1928, meaning it had almost exactly doubled in under two years. After the peak on September 3, the index spent most of September and October falling in small increments and partial recoveries — the pattern that typically keeps investors holding on, each decline seeming like the dip before the next rise. By the time Black Thursday arrived on October 24, the Dow had already lost about 17 percent from its peak, but almost nobody framed it that way.

events.label: Black Thursday
events.description: On Thursday, October 24, 1929, panic selling swept the New York Stock Exchange and a record 12.9 million shares changed hands; a pool of the country's leading bankers publicly bought shares that afternoon to signal confidence, and it worked — for exactly one weekend.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The banker pool that stepped in on Black Thursday was organized by Thomas Lamont of J.P. Morgan and included the heads of the major New York banks; they each contributed roughly $40 million to buy shares visibly on the floor, a tactic that had actually worked in the Panic of 1907. The gesture sent prices back up somewhat and the weekend press was full of reassurances that the worst was over. When the market opened Monday, it became clear the pool's purchases had only delayed the reckoning — the banks quietly unloaded their purchases into the brief Monday rally.

events.label: Black Tuesday and the Crash
events.description: On Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the dam broke: 16.4 million shares were dumped in the single worst day in the exchange's history, the ticker ran hours behind actual prices, and margin calls forced selling that triggered more margin calls in a self-feeding collapse that erased roughly $30 billion in paper wealth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ticker tape — the machine that printed stock prices on a narrow paper strip — ran so far behind actual trading that investors were executing sell orders based on prices that had already fallen another 10 or 20 percent. Some estimates put the delay at two and a half hours at the worst point, meaning traders literally did not know what price they were selling at. The $30 billion in losses over the worst two weeks was more than the entire cost of U.S. participation in World War I, and the market would not return to its September 1929 peak until 1954.

events.label: The morning after the Crash
events.description: Hoover and the bankers insisted prosperity was 'just around the corner'; the market briefly rallied into 1930 before collapsing for real. The Crash did not cause the Great Depression alone, but it ended the Roaring Twenties — and the next era begins here.

events.label: Jim Crow at its height
events.description: Jim Crow was the body of state laws and social customs built across the South after Reconstruction's collapse in 1877, enforcing racial segregation, stripping Black men of the vote through poll taxes and rigged literacy tests, and backing the whole system with the threat of lynching.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Supreme Court gave Jim Crow its constitutional seal of approval in 1896's Plessy v. Ferguson, ruling that 'separate but equal' facilities were lawful — a doctrine that stood for fifty-eight years. The laws drew their name from a minstrel-show song, 'Jump Jim Crow,' making a racist caricature the face of an entire legal architecture. Jim Crow laws did not die with the Civil Rights Act; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was required to dislodge the disfranchisement machinery ninety-five years after the Fifteenth Amendment had supposedly already guaranteed the vote.

events.label: The Progressive Era's legacy
events.description: The Progressive Era (roughly 1900–1917) was the reform backlash against Gilded Age inequality: it gave the country the federal income tax, the Federal Reserve (the national central bank created in 1913), direct election of senators, the first federal food and drug regulations, and two constitutional amendments — Prohibition and women's suffrage — that shaped the entire twenties.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Federal Reserve's founding in 1913 was itself a response to the Panic of 1907, when a single banker, J.P. Morgan, had to personally organize a private bailout of the American financial system because no government institution existed to do it. Progressivism was genuinely contradictory: many of its most prominent reformers were also ardent eugenicists and nativists, and 'efficiency' in the Progressive vocabulary sometimes meant excluding the poor or immigrant from democratic participation. The direct election of senators, ratified as the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913, replaced the old system where state legislatures chose senators — a mechanism corporations had long used to buy Senate seats outright.

events.label: The Gilded Age inheritance
events.description: The decades after 1877 — the Gilded Age, a name Mark Twain gave to the era's glittering surface over corrupt foundations — built the transcontinental railroads, the steel and oil empires, and the giant monopolistic corporations that were the industrial machine the twenties ran on.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The term 'trust' came from an actual legal maneuver: shareholders of competing companies handed their stock to a single board of trustees, which then ran all the firms as one combine while they technically remained separate — Standard Oil's trust structure was the model. Carnegie's steel company and Rockefeller's Standard Oil each controlled around 25–30% of their respective industries by the late 1890s. The Gilded Age also produced the first sustained labor organizing in American history, including the Knights of Labor, which briefly had 700,000 members in the 1880s.

events.label: America's World War
events.description: The United States stayed out of the European war for nearly three years after 1914, then entered in April 1917, mobilized four million men, shipped two million to France, and fought through the war's last brutal months, losing about 116,000 dead — roughly half in combat, the rest mostly to disease.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The immediate trigger for the declaration of war was Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917 and the interception of the Zimmermann Telegram, a secret German proposal to Mexico offering it Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona in exchange for attacking the United States. The war transformed America's financial position: entering as a debtor nation, it exited as the world's leading creditor, owed about $10 billion by Britain and France — a reversal that gave the U.S. extraordinary leverage over European economic policy throughout the twenties.

events.label: Wartime repression and its hangover
events.description: The Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a federal crime to say or print anything that obstructed military recruiting or cast the government in a negative light — meaning a public speech urging draft resistance was itself the prosecutable act, no actual spying required.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Socialist Party leader Eugene Debs was sentenced to ten years in prison for a single speech in Canton, Ohio, and ran for president in 1920 from his cell at the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary, receiving nearly a million votes. The Sedition Act was so broadly written that it made it a crime to use 'disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language' about the United States government, the flag, or the military uniform. Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer kept the machinery running after the war ended, using it to deport hundreds of foreign-born radicals in the 1919–1920 Palmer Raids without criminal trial.

events.label: Harding pardons Eugene Debs
events.description: Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs, who had run for president from his federal prison cell in 1920 and received nearly a million votes, was released on Christmas Day 1921 when President Harding commuted his sentence — a signal that the Red Scare had burned itself out.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Debs had been sentenced to ten years under the Sedition Act of 1918 for a speech in Canton, Ohio, criticizing U.S. involvement in World War I. He ran his 1920 presidential campaign with the slogan 'From the Prison Cell to the White House' and received 913,693 votes — roughly 3.4% of the total — the strongest third-party showing of the election. Harding not only commuted his sentence but invited him to the White House for a personal meeting, which Debs called the most moving experience of his life.

events.label: The Teapot Dome trials
events.description: Albert Fall was convicted of bribery in 1929 and became the first U.S. cabinet officer ever imprisoned for crimes committed in office. In a verdict that became a national punchline, the oilman convicted of nothing — Harry Sinclair — was acquitted of paying the bribe that Fall was convicted of receiving.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sinclair was acquitted of bribery but did serve time — 6.5 months — for contempt of the Senate and contempt of court after he hired private detectives to shadow the jury during his trial. Fall, the one convicted of actually taking the money, was too ill to serve his full sentence and was released early; he died broke in 1944.

events.label: Sacco and Vanzetti executed
events.description: On August 23, 1927, after seven years of worldwide protests, petitions from figures including Albert Einstein and H.G. Wells, and multiple failed appeals, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were electrocuted at Charlestown State Prison in Massachusetts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The case drew demonstrations on multiple continents; protests erupted in London, Paris, Buenos Aires, and Tokyo in the days before the execution. Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a proclamation in 1977 — fifty years later — declaring that the men had been unfairly tried and that any stigma should be removed from their names. The ballistics question remains genuinely open: later analysis suggested Sacco may have fired the fatal shots while Vanzetti probably did not.

events.label: The Kellogg–Briand Pact
events.description: In August 1928 the U.S. and France led 15 nations in signing a pact 'renouncing war as an instrument of national policy.' Toothless but earnest, it captured the decade's war-weary idealism and its retreat from world affairs.

events.label: Asian exclusion completed
events.description: The 1924 act completed the exclusion of Asian immigrants by barring anyone 'ineligible to citizenship' — a category defined by earlier racial naturalization law that courts had already ruled included Japanese and South Asian immigrants, effectively extending Chinese exclusion to the entire continent.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The legal mechanism ran through a 1790 statute limiting naturalization to 'free white persons'; two 1920s Supreme Court rulings confirmed that Japanese (Ozawa v. U.S., 1922) and South Asian Indians (U.S. v. Bhagat Singh Thind, 1923) did not legally qualify as white, which the 1924 act then used as the trigger for outright exclusion. Japan had a 'Gentlemen's Agreement' with the U.S. since 1907 under which it voluntarily restricted emigration; the 1924 act abrogated that arrangement unilaterally, and the insult was felt acutely in Tokyo, feeding the nationalist grievance that would fester across the following two decades.

events.label: Nativism and '100% Americanism'
events.description: The '100% Americanism' movement of the early 1920s fused anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic, anti-Jewish, and anti-radical feeling into a political force that powered the Klan, the immigration restriction acts, and the Red Scare — essentially, organized cultural anxiety about who counted as a real American.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The phrase '100% American' was promoted by wartime loyalty campaigns that had made hyphenated identity suspect; after the war, the energy turned inward against peacetime 'alien' influences. Nativist politics in this era were bipartisan — many Progressive-era reformers supported immigration restriction as a labor and eugenics measure, not just as ethnic hostility.

events.label: The Muscle Shoals fight
events.description: Senator George Norris fought through the twenties to keep the government's wartime Muscle Shoals dam and nitrate plant public; Coolidge and Hoover wanted it sold to private interests like Henry Ford. The deadlocked fight set up the later public-power debate.

events.label: Anti-evolution laws spread
events.description: Despite the national mockery of the Scopes trial, the fundamentalists won the longer fight: Mississippi passed an anti-evolution law in 1926, Arkansas in 1928, and major textbook publishers quietly removed or diluted Darwin from biology books for decades rather than risk losing Southern school-board contracts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tennessee's Butler Act was not repealed until 1967, and it took a Supreme Court ruling (Epperson v. Arkansas, 1968) to finally strike down Arkansas's law as unconstitutional. The fundamentalists' strategic response to Dayton was not to disappear but to build a parallel institutional world — their own colleges, publishers, and radio stations — that would re-enter mainstream American politics at scale in the 1970s and 1980s. The textbook publishers' self-censorship meant that millions of American students learned almost nothing about evolution for roughly 40 years after Scopes.

events.label: 'I do not choose to run'
events.description: On August 2, 1927 — the fourth anniversary of his father's lamplit oath — Coolidge handed reporters a single typed sentence reading 'I do not choose to run for President in nineteen twenty eight' and walked away without answering questions. He left Washington before the Crash he'd helped set up arrived.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The terse announcement was so unexpected that several of Coolidge's own Cabinet members heard about it from the press. His teenage son Calvin Jr. had died in 1924 from a blood infection caused by a blister from playing tennis on the White House lawn — a loss Coolidge later wrote had haunted his entire presidency. Historians debate whether he sensed the boom was unsustainable, but the timing made him the luckiest man in American politics: Herbert Hoover inherited both the White House and the Crash within 18 months.

events.label: Politics on the air
events.description: The 1924 Democratic and Republican conventions were the first to be broadcast nationally, letting the country hear political theater it had previously only read about in next-day newspaper summaries. The 1924 Democratic convention — which took 103 ballots to pick a candidate — became an inadvertent advertisement for the chaos of the party process.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 103-ballot Democratic deadlock in 1924 was so brutal and so publicly audible that it may have cost the party the election; the nation's first real-time exposure to convention horsetrading was not flattering. Coolidge, who barely spoke in public, found radio congenial precisely because it rewarded restraint and punished the blustering oratory that had filled outdoor rally grounds — an early demonstration that each new medium selects for a different political personality.

events.label: The 103-ballot Democratic convention
events.description: The 1924 Democratic National Convention in New York deadlocked for a record 103 ballots over 16 days — the longest in U.S. history — pitting the Klan-backed William McAdoo against Catholic Al Smith, and producing the extraordinary spectacle of a major party's delegates voting, by the thinnest possible margin, not to officially condemn the Ku Klux Klan by name.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The anti-Klan plank lost by roughly 542 to 541 votes out of more than a thousand fractional delegate votes — a margin of less than one full delegate. The convention earned the nickname 'The Klanbake' in the press. The eventual compromise nominee, John W. Davis, lost the general election in a landslide to Calvin Coolidge, partly because the convention had so thoroughly exposed Democratic divisions.

events.label: Religious broadcasting begins
events.description: In the early 1920s, religious broadcasters — led by figures like Aimee Semple McPherson in Los Angeles and Father Charles Coughlin in Detroit — discovered that radio could reach audiences no church building ever could, beginning a marriage between evangelism and mass media that would define American religious life for the rest of the century.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Father Charles Coughlin began broadcasting from Royal Oak, Michigan in 1926, eventually attracting an estimated 30 million weekly listeners in the 1930s — one of the largest audiences of any broadcaster in the world. The Federal Radio Commission (established 1927) initially reserved few frequencies for religious broadcasters, pushing many onto the airwaves at odd hours, but the audience grew anyway. By 1930 there were over 60 religious radio stations in the United States, a number that would multiply many times over in subsequent decades.

events.label: The Air Commerce Act
events.description: The Air Commerce Act of 1926 gave the federal government authority to license pilots and aircraft and build airways, creating the regulatory base of commercial aviation just as Lindbergh's flight set off the boom.

events.label: Television's first demonstrations
events.description: Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first electronic television image in 1927 and AT&T demonstrated TV in 1927; the technology that would dominate the next era was already being born inside the radio decade.

events.label: Goddard's liquid-fuel rocket
events.description: On March 16, 1926, Robert Goddard launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket from a Massachusetts farm; it flew 41 feet. Ridiculed at the time, it was the seed of twentieth-century rocketry.

events.label: Insulin and the medical twenties
events.description: Insulin, first used on a patient in 1922, turned diabetes from a death sentence into a managed disease and signaled the decade's real scientific advance amid the boom. Medicine, like industry, was being transformed by the laboratory.

events.label: The first nationally broadcast trial
events.description: Chicago's WGN radio station ran telephone lines to the Dayton courtroom and broadcast the Scopes trial live, making it the first American trial heard in real time by a national audience — a moment when a local legal dispute became a shared national event simply because the technology existed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: WGN stood for 'World's Greatest Newspaper,' the call letters assigned by the Chicago Tribune, which owned the station and whose reporters also covered the trial in print. The broadcast reached audiences in living rooms across the country who had never set foot in Tennessee, fundamentally changing what a 'public' trial meant. Radio coverage also meant that Darrow's questioning of Bryan — including his stumbles and contradictions — was heard in real time rather than filtered through the next day's newspaper.

events.label: The Osage murders
events.description: Wealthy from oil under their Oklahoma land, dozens of Osage were murdered in the early twenties by whites scheming to inherit their headrights. The new Bureau of Investigation's case helped build J. Edgar Hoover's FBI.

events.label: The Snyder–Gray murder trial
events.description: The 1927 trial of Ruth Snyder and Judd Gray for murdering her husband was a tabloid sensation; a photographer's hidden camera caught her execution for the Daily News front page. It captured the decade's appetite for crime as mass entertainment.

events.label: The machinery of celebrity
events.description: Lindbergh's 1927 flight showed how radio, tabloids, and newsreels could transform a quiet unknown into a global celebrity overnight — fame itself became an industrial product in the twenties, manufactured by the same media machine that sold cars and soap.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The concept of 'celebrity' as mass-media-manufactured fame rather than earned renown was genuinely new to the 1920s; earlier famous figures had required years of accumulated public exposure. Rudolph Valentino's 1926 death triggered what newspapers called 'mass hysteria' — a new and alarming phenomenon of collective grief for someone most mourners had never met. The same machinery that built Lindbergh up proved equally capable of destroying reputations, a dynamic that would play out in scandal coverage from the era's tabloid press.

events.label: Women in the modern workforce
events.description: More women worked for wages in the twenties — as typists, telephone operators, clerks, and salesgirls — but mostly in low-paid 'pink-collar' jobs, and most quit at marriage. The vote had not delivered economic equality.

events.label: Margaret Sanger's birth-control movement
events.description: Margaret Sanger — nurse, writer, and birth-control activist — built the movement that would eventually become Planned Parenthood, genuinely expanding women's control over their lives even as her advocacy was entangled with the eugenics ideas that pervaded the era's reform movements.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sanger had been arrested in 1916 for operating an earlier illegal birth-control clinic in Brooklyn, which was shut down after nine days; the legal clinic came later after sustained legal battles. She was instrumental decades later in funding the research that produced the first oral contraceptive pill, approved by the FDA in 1960. Her embrace of eugenics — including support for sterilization programs — remains a defining controversy in her legacy.

events.label: How the car remade society
events.description: Within one decade the car moved from rich man's toy to family necessity, and ordinary American life reorganized itself around it — not just commuting but dating, churchgoing, vacations, and the physical shape of cities. No previous consumer object had reshaped a society's physical geography so fast.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The private car created what sociologists called "auto camping" — middle-class families driving to national parks and sleeping in tents beside the road — which exploded park visitation in the twenties and prompted the National Park Service to build its first vehicle roads. Police reported a sharp rise in what they called "automobile bandits" — criminals who could now commit crimes in one town and be in another before anyone organized a response, creating the first generation of what would become the FBI's focus on interstate crime. The car also quietly extended courtship out of parents' supervision: by 1925 Muncie judges were seeing juvenile cases tied to "joy riding" that had no legal category five years earlier.

events.label: The Middletown study
events.description: Robert and Helen Lynd's 1929 book 'Middletown' — a full sociological study of Muncie, Indiana — documented in careful detail how the car, the factory, the radio, and advertising had transformed an ordinary American town across a single generation. It remains the decade's most thorough self-portrait.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Lynds chose Muncie partly because it was a predominantly white, native-born city — they wanted to study 'American' change without the variable of recent immigration, a methodological choice that itself reflects the decade's racial anxieties. One of their key findings was that the automobile had almost entirely replaced church and family as the organizing institution of young people's social life — a finding that scandalized readers in 1929. The Lynds returned for a follow-up study in the Depression, publishing 'Middletown in Transition' in 1937, which found the boom's consumer habits had survived remarkably intact even in hard times.

events.label: Fads and crazes
events.description: Mah-jongg, crossword puzzles, flagpole sitting, dance marathons, and Coué's 'every day in every way' auto-suggestion swept the decade. Mass media could now make a national craze out of almost anything within weeks.

events.label: Jazz goes national
events.description: Radio, phonograph records, and the Great Migration carried New Orleans and Chicago jazz to white dance halls, college campuses, and Europe within a decade. Older critics called it degenerate; the young made it the sound of modern life.

events.label: Paul Whiteman, the 'King of Jazz'
events.description: Bandleader Paul Whiteman sold a polished, orchestrated 'symphonic jazz' to mass white audiences and was crowned the 'King of Jazz' — a marketing of Black music that made him rich while its originators went largely unpaid.

events.label: The rise of college culture
events.description: College enrollment doubled in the twenties, and the campus — football, fraternities, raccoon coats, the 'collegiate' style — became a mass cultural model. Higher education was becoming a middle-class expectation, not an elite preserve.

events.label: The Anti-Saloon League's power
events.description: The Anti-Saloon League, founded in 1893, perfected a single-issue lobbying model: endorse or destroy any candidate of either party based solely on their 'wet' or 'dry' vote, channeling Protestant church networks into a disciplined voting machine that drove Prohibition into the Constitution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The League's chief strategist, Wayne Wheeler, personally drafted the Volstead Act that enforced the amendment — making the same organization responsible for writing both the law and its enforcement mechanism. Wheeler's approach of electing single-issue 'dry' politicians regardless of party became a template studied by later advocacy groups across the political spectrum.

events.label: The Wickersham Commission begins
events.description: President Hoover convened the Wickersham Commission in 1929 to study Prohibition enforcement; its 1931 report exhaustively documented that the law was unenforceable and failing — then, astonishingly, recommended it be kept, with several commissioners privately contradicting the official conclusion in individual dissenting notes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The commission's chairman was former U.S. Attorney General George Wickersham, lending it significant prestige. The final report's internal contradictions — individual commissioners essentially saying the opposite of the group's official recommendation — were widely mocked in the press. The episode became a symbol of political paralysis: even a body charged with honestly evaluating Prohibition couldn't bring itself to say plainly what its own evidence showed.

events.label: Hoover's 'associative state'
events.description: Herbert Hoover transformed the Commerce Department from a backwater into the most dynamic agency in Washington, pushing industrial standardization, trade associations, radio spectrum regulation, and commercial aviation — all without running the economy directly or leaving it alone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before entering government, Hoover had organized food relief for occupied Belgium during World War I, feeding roughly 10 million people, and then ran the wartime Food Administration — achievements that made him one of the most admired men in America. His Commerce Department reduced the number of standard brick sizes from 44 to 4 and standardized everything from auto tires to bed springs, which economists credit with measurable productivity gains.

events.label: The National Origins quota takes effect
events.description: The full National Origins Formula took effect in July 1929, capping total immigration at about 150,000 people a year — down from over 800,000 in 1921 alone — with slots apportioned to mirror the ethnic composition of the 1890 U.S. population. The formula governed who could enter the country until the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 finally replaced it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 'national origins' calculation itself was a bureaucratic nightmare: officials had to work backward through census records and immigration data to estimate the ancestry of the entire U.S. population as of 1890, an exercise that took years and was disputed throughout. Britain and Ireland together received about 65,000 slots — nearly half the entire annual ceiling — while countries like Italy and Poland received a few thousand each. The 1929 date of final implementation also meant the formula kicked in just as the Great Depression began, though by then legal immigration had already been throttled to near nothing.

events.label: Amos 'n' Andy and network programming
events.description: Amos 'n' Andy debuted on Chicago radio in 1928 and became the first national blockbuster of the broadcast era: the show was so popular that movie theaters reportedly interrupted screenings to pipe it in so audiences wouldn't go home to listen. Its premise was two white performers, Freeman Gosden and Charles Correll, performing exaggerated 'Black dialect' caricatures — the minstrel tradition now beamed to millions every night.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At its peak Amos 'n' Andy drew an estimated 40 million listeners per broadcast, roughly a third of the country. The NAACP campaigned against it from the start, but NBC and its sponsors dismissed the objections — the show was too profitable to touch. When it moved to television in 1951 with a Black cast, the NAACP successfully pressured CBS to cancel it after two seasons, making it one of the first shows pulled due to organized civil rights pressure.

events.label: Mickey Mouse debuts
events.description: Walt Disney's Steamboat Willie, premiering November 1928, introduced Mickey Mouse and synchronized cartoon sound. A new American mass-entertainment empire began in the same months as the bull market's final surge.

events.label: Show Boat changes the musical
events.description: Kern and Hammerstein's Show Boat (December 1927) wove a serious story of race and miscegenation into a Broadway musical, with 'Ol' Man River' sung by a Black performer. It pointed the American musical toward drama, not just revue.

events.label: An American modernism
events.description: Georgia O'Keeffe, Edward Hopper, and the Stieglitz circle built a distinctly American modern art in the twenties, while Harlem's Aaron Douglas gave the renaissance its visual style. The decade asked what American culture, freed from Europe, looked like.

events.label: Women, drink, and Prohibition's reversal
events.description: Pauline Sabin, a Republican socialite and former supporter of Prohibition, founded the Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform (WONPR) in 1929, demolishing the dry coalition's central claim that American women were the movement's backbone. Within two years WONPR had over a million members.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sabin argued that Prohibition had made drinking more attractive to young people, not less — that the forbidden glamour of the speakeasy was doing more to encourage youth drinking than open saloons ever had. Her organization's rapid growth to over a million members outpaced the Women's Christian Temperance Union, the leading pro-Prohibition women's group, in just a few years, directly undermining the moral authority the dry side had relied on.

events.label: The ignored warnings
events.description: A small number of people said the market was a bubble and were treated accordingly: economist Roger Babson was publicly mocked after predicting a crash in September 1929, while Yale's Irving Fisher declared stocks had reached 'a permanently high plateau' days before the collapse.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Fisher's reputation never fully recovered — his phrase 'permanently high plateau' is still taught in economics courses as a textbook example of peak-euphoria forecasting. What is less often noted is that Fisher had his own money in the market and lost a personal fortune estimated at several million dollars in the crash. Babson, by contrast, had been warning of a crash for over a year before his September 5, 1929 speech; the initial market drop on the day of his warning was briefly called the 'Babson Break,' but the recovery that followed made him look alarmist — until it didn't.

events.label: The banking system's hidden fragility
events.description: Beneath the whole decade's prosperity sat a banking system of roughly 25,000 mostly small, undiversified local banks with no deposit insurance — a structure designed to fail when confidence cracked, and the reason the Crash became a depression rather than a recession.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike today's system where the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) guarantees your deposits up to $250,000, 1929 depositors had no protection at all: if your bank failed, your savings were simply gone. The U.S. had no national deposit insurance and resisted it — the banking lobby argued it would reward reckless banks. Between 1930 and 1933, roughly 9,000 banks failed, wiping out the savings of millions of ordinary families who had never bought a single share of stock. Congress finally passed deposit insurance in 1933, and there has not been a systemic bank-run panic in the United States since.

events.label: The Young Plan
events.description: The 1929 Young Plan again rescheduled German reparations and depended on continued American lending. When the Crash cut off U.S. capital, the circular debt structure of the twenties collapsed and pulled down the world economy.

events.label: The American Legion founded
events.description: Veterans of the World War founded the American Legion in 1919; it became a powerful, conservative, anti-radical lobby and a fixture of the era's '100% American' politics, while also pressing for the soldiers' bonus that would explode in 1932.

events.label: The Centralia massacre
events.description: On Armistice Day 1919, an American Legion parade and the radical Industrial Workers of the World clashed in Centralia, Washington; the gunfight and the lynching of the IWW member Wesley Everest fused the Red Scare with veteran-led violence.

events.label: The West Virginia mine wars
events.description: In August–September 1921, roughly 10,000 armed West Virginia coal miners marched on Logan and Mingo counties to break the coal operators' private armies and forced company towns — towns entirely owned and controlled by the mine company. The Battle of Blair Mountain was the largest armed labor uprising in U.S. history; it ended only when the Army deployed aircraft and federal troops against the miners.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The miners faced not just hired company gunmen but a sheriff, Don Chafin, who was on the coal operators' payroll and commanded his own private army of around 3,000 men. Army aircraft flew reconnaissance and reportedly dropped surplus WWI gas and explosive bombs on the miners — the first aerial bombing of American citizens on U.S. soil. The union was crushed: United Mine Workers membership in West Virginia collapsed from around 50,000 to nearly zero in the aftermath.

events.label: The 1922 railway shopmen's strike
events.description: Some 400,000 railway shop workers struck in 1922 against wage cuts; a sweeping federal injunction broke it and signaled the decade's hostile turn against organized labor. Union membership fell through the prosperous twenties.

events.label: The Taft Court and business
events.description: Chief Justice William Howard Taft's Supreme Court (1921–30) struck down child-labor laws and minimum-wage laws and limited union power, writing the decade's pro-business ideology into constitutional law. It was the legal arm of 'the business of America.'

events.label: The immigrant city before the door closed
events.description: Between roughly 1880 and 1924 about 25 million people immigrated to the United States, shifting in source from Britain and Germany to southern and eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, Russians, and millions of Jews fleeing Russian pogroms (organized mob massacres of Jewish communities). The 1920 census was the first to find more Americans in cities than on farms.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The new immigrants arrived in numbers that dwarfed earlier waves: in peak year 1907 alone, 1.3 million people entered the country. Because they settled in the industrial cities rather than spreading onto farms, they were visible in a way earlier immigrants had not been — a fact that powered the nativist backlash that produced the 1924 Immigration Act. The 1920 census's urban-majority finding was close: 51.2% urban to 48.8% rural, a margin of about 1.4 million people in a country of 106 million.

events.label: The Rosewood massacre
events.description: In January 1923 a white mob destroyed the Black town of Rosewood, Florida, after a false assault accusation, killing an uncertain number and driving out the survivors for good. It was one of several twenties race massacres long erased from public memory.

events.label: Black institutions in the Jim Crow twenties
events.description: Black colleges, the Black press, the church, and Black-owned businesses expanded in the twenties, North and South, building the institutional base that the civil-rights movement would later mobilize. Survival under Jim Crow was itself organized.

events.label: Transcontinental air mail
events.description: Regular coast-to-coast air mail began in 1924, cutting cross-country delivery to about 30 hours. The 1925 Kelly Act handed the routes to private carriers, founding the companies that became United, American, and TWA.

events.label: A law for the poor
events.description: The rich kept stocked cellars and drank at private clubs; Prohibition fell hardest on working people and immigrants whose saloons were raided and whose bootleg liquor was deadliest. The class double standard fueled the case for repeal.

events.label: The Jones Law stiffens Prohibition
events.description: The Jones Law of 1929 transformed first-offense bootlegging from a minor violation into a felony (a serious crime with prison time, as opposed to a misdemeanor fine), punishable by up to five years and a $10,000 fine — the dry movement's attempt to save Prohibition by making the penalties harsher even as public support was collapsing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The law was nicknamed the 'Five-and-Ten' for its maximum penalties. Critics pointed out that it made casual bootleggers eligible for stiffer sentences than most violent crimes carried at the time, and juries in wet cities became even less willing to convict. Congress passed it as a show of resolve, but it accelerated rather than reversed the erosion of Prohibition's legitimacy.

events.label: Stock pools and insider rigging
events.description: Operators secretly pooled money to pump a stock with rumor and wash trades, then dumped it on the public — perfectly legal in the twenties. The unregulated, manipulable market of the decade is why the New Deal created the SEC afterward.

events.label: RCA, the bull market's glamour stock
events.description: Radio Corporation of America rose from about $85 to $549 in 1928 alone without ever paying a dividend, the decade's emblem of a price driven by the future people imagined rather than earnings. It cratered in the Crash.

events.label: The Empire State Building announced
events.description: Plans for the 102-story Empire State Building were unveiled in 1929 to top the Chrysler Building; ground broke in 1930. Conceived at the peak of the boom, it opened into the Depression two-thirds empty, nicknamed the 'Empty State Building.'

events.label: The car and the national parks
events.description: Auto tourism transformed the national parks in the twenties: visitor numbers multiplied, the Park Service built roads and lodges, and the cross-country motor trip became a middle-class ritual. Leisure itself was becoming an industry.

events.label: The Mer Rouge Klan murders
events.description: In August 1922 hooded men seized two Mer Rouge, Louisiana, men — F. Watt Daniel and Thomas Richards — who had spoken out against the local Klan, tortured and killed them, and dumped their bodies in a lake; they surfaced in December. Despite fifty witnesses naming Klan members including the local sheriff and district attorney, a Klan-infiltrated grand jury dismissed the case for 'insufficient evidence.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The bodies were only found after a mysterious underwater explosion disturbed the lake bottom where they had been weighed down. A state investigation subpoenaed over 200 witnesses and revealed that the local Klan chapter, No. 34, had essentially merged with local government. The case drew national press attention and became one of the first documented examples of a government body being so thoroughly captured by the Klan that prosecution was structurally impossible.

events.label: Sylvia Beach publishes Ulysses
events.description: In 1922, American expatriate Sylvia Beach published James Joyce's Ulysses from her Left Bank Paris bookshop, Shakespeare and Company, after every commercial house refused it and American obscenity law banned it — one of the most consequential gambles in literary publishing history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Beach had only met Joyce a few months before agreeing to publish Ulysses, with no prior publishing experience whatsoever. She financed the first edition of 1,000 copies largely through advance subscriptions from readers. Copies smuggled into the United States were routinely seized and burned by U.S. Customs; the novel remained legally banned in America until a federal court ruling in 1933.

events.label: Frankfurter and the report on Justice Department lawlessness
events.description: In 1920, Harvard law professor Felix Frankfurter led a group of prominent lawyers who published a detailed report documenting the Justice Department's illegal conduct during the Palmer Raids, helping turn elite legal opinion against the Red Scare.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Frankfurter was a Vienna-born civil-liberties advocate who happened to live on the same Washington block as Palmer when the anarchist bomb went off on the Attorney General's steps in 1919 — a neighbor of the very event that triggered the crackdown he then helped expose. He went on to become a Supreme Court justice in 1939, where he served until 1962. The report he co-authored was one of the earliest systematic uses of legal scholarship as a civil-rights tool.

events.label: The end of the Roaring Twenties
events.description: The Roaring Twenties — the decade that built the modern consumer economy, broadcast culture, and car culture, and made in Harlem a body of art that outlasted everything else it produced — ended in eleven days of falling numbers in October 1929, the ticker running hours behind the truth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Dow Jones did not return to its September 1929 peak of 381 until November 1954 — 25 years later. At its absolute bottom in July 1932 the Dow hit 41, a drop of almost 90 percent from the peak. The generation that survived the Depression and the war that followed became marked by a lifelong distrust of stock markets and credit; personal savings rates and caution about debt that puzzled economists in the postwar decades were a direct behavioral inheritance of what happened in the eleven days this event describes.
